<meta>This page continues a philosophical argument concerning the flaws of human reason and the necessity for a total "Restoration" of knowledge. ...diffuse, and recklessly abstracted from **Realities**; nor is there less whim and inconstancy in the secondary and remaining steps. From this it follows that all that **Human Reason**, which we use in the **Investigation of Nature**, is not well assembled and built, but is like some magnificent **Structure** without a foundation. For while men admire and celebrate the **False powers of the Mind**; they pass over and lose its **True powers** (which could exist, if the proper aids were applied to it, and if the mind itself were obedient to **Realities**, and did not powerlessly insult them <note>Bacon is critiquing the tendency of philosophers to impose their own theories onto nature rather than observing nature as it actually is.</note>) they pass over and lose.

One thing remained: that the matter be attempted anew, with better safeguards; and that there be a universal <term>Restoration</term> <note>original: "Instauratio." This refers to Bacon's famous project to overhaul the entire system of human knowledge and scientific inquiry.</note> of the **Sciences**, the **Arts**, and all **Human Learning**, raised from the proper **Foundations**. This undertaking may indeed seem like something infinite and beyond mortal strength; yet, in the handling, it will be found sane and sober, more so than what has been done until now. For this path has an actual exit. In those things, however, which are now being done regarding the **Sciences**, there is a kind of **Giddiness**, a perpetual **Agitation**, and a **Circling** <note>He characterizes the scholarship of his time—specifically Medieval Scholasticism—as a repetitive cycle that produces no new discoveries.</note>.

Nor does it escape him <note>Bacon frequently refers to himself in the third person in these prefaces to lend the work a sense of objective gravity.</note> in what great solitude this **Experiment** is conducted, and how hard and incredible it is to win people's trust. Nevertheless, he thought that neither the cause nor himself should be abandoned, but rather he should attempt and enter the **Way**, which is the only one open to the **Human Mind**. For it is better to give a **Beginning** to a **Matter** which can have an **End**, than to remain in those things which have no end, in per-

*Most Serene and Potent King,*

[Decorative initial P]erhaps your Majesty might accuse me of theft, in that I have stolen from your affairs <note>Bacon was serving as Lord Chancellor at the time, the highest legal office in England, and thus "stole" time from his royal duties to write philosophy</note> as much time as was needed for these labors. I have no defense to offer, for time once spent cannot be restored; unless, perhaps, that which was withdrawn from your business may be credited to the memory of your name and the honor of your age, provided these writings are of any worth. 

They are certainly quite new—entirely new in their very nature—yet they are drawn from a most ancient model: the World itself, and the Nature of Things and of the Mind. I myself (to confess frankly) am inclined to regard this Work more as a child of Time than of Wit <note>original: "partu Temporis, quam Ingenii." This is a famous expression of Bacon's humility, suggesting that his "New Instrument" of science is a natural result of the era's progress rather than his own personal genius</note>. For the only thing truly remarkable about it is that the first sparks of the matter, and such great doubts regarding those ideas which have long prevailed <note>This refers to the "received" wisdom of the Middle Ages, particularly the reliance on Aristotle's logic</note>, should have occurred to someone's mind...

...to have been able to come forth. The rest follows not unwillingly. But there is undoubtedly "Chance" (as we call it) and something like the "Fortuitous" involved no less in what men think than in what they do and say.

Truly, I want this Chance (of which I speak) to be understood in this way: if there is anything good in what I offer, let it be attributed to the immense Mercy and divine Goodness, and to the Prosperity of your times. To these I have served in life with the most sincere affection, and in death I shall perhaps have brought it about that these things may shine before Posterity, this new torch having been lit in the darkness of Philosophy. <note>In this period, "Philosophy" usually refers to "Natural Philosophy," which we now call Science.</note> Rightly, this *Regeneration* and *Restoration* <note>original: *Instauratio*</note> of the Sciences is owed to the Times of a King most wise and learned of all.

There remains a Petition, not unworthy of your Majesty, and most of all contributing to the matter at hand. It establishes the author's premise: that human knowledge has stagnated because people either overestimate current achievements or underestimate their own potential for discovery.</meta>

# ->F R A N C I S<-
# ->O F<-
# ->V E R U L A M’ S<-
## Great Restoration.

### ->P R E F A C E.<-

*On the state of the Sciences: that it is not prosperous, or greatly advanced; and that a path entirely different from that known to our predecessors must be opened to the human Intellect, and other aids provided, so that the mind may exercise its rightful authority over the Nature of things.*

[Decorative initial V] It seems to me <note>The original Latin "nobis" (to us) is the 'authorial we,' common in formal writing of this period.</note> that men do not rightly know either their resources or their powers; but rather believe more than is fair of the former, and less of the latter. Thus it happens that they either value the accepted arts at an insane price <note>original: "insanis pretiis"; meaning they overvalue existing knowledge to an irrational degree.</note> and seek nothing further; or, despising themselves more than is just, they waste their strength on trivial matters, and do not put it to the test in those things which concern the heart of the matter. Therefore, the Sciences also have their Pillars <note>Bacon refers here to the "Pillars of Hercules," the traditional limit of the Mediterranean world, symbolizing the perceived limits of human knowledge that he intends to sail beyond.</note>, as if fixed by fate; since men are moved by neither desire nor hope to penetrate further. And, since the belief in abundance <note>original: "opinio copiae"; the mistaken idea that we already possess all the knowledge we need.</note> is among the greatest causes of poverty; and since because of confidence in what we currently have, true aids for the future are neglected; it is useful, and indeed necessary, that from those things which have been discovered so far...

<summary>In this preface, Francis Bacon argues that human scientific progress is stalled by a false sense of satisfaction with current knowledge and a lack of confidence in new discovery. He calls for a complete overhaul of how the human mind approaches the study of nature.</summary>

<keywords>Francis Bacon, Great Restoration, philosophy of science, human intellect, Pillars of Hercules, Instauratio Magna, scientific method</keywords>

--- Page 10 ---
<meta>This page contains the opening of the Preface to Francis Bacon's Great Instauration (Instauratio Magna), likely the 1620 edition. It follows the common early modern theme of critiquing Scholasticism in favor of a new empirical method.</meta>

# PREFACE.

...at the very threshold of our work (leaving aside all ambiguity and speaking quite openly), let the excess of honor and admiration be removed. This serves as a useful warning, lest men overestimate or over-celebrate either the quantity or the usefulness of the knowledge they currently possess. For if anyone looks more closely into that great variety of books in which the Arts and Sciences pride themselves, they will find everywhere infinite repetitions of the same thing—different in how they are handled, but already claimed by previous discovery. Thus, things that seem numerous at first glance are found, upon examination, to be few. 

And regarding utility <note>Bacon defines "utility" as the practical application of knowledge to improve the human condition.</note>, it must be said: that wisdom which we have drawn primarily from the Greeks <note>original: "à Græcis potiſſimum hauſimus." Bacon refers here to the Aristotelian and Platonic traditions that dominated the universities of his time.</note> seems to be a kind of childhood of Science, possessing the traits of children: it is quick to chatter, but weak and immature when it comes to generating <note>In this context, "generating" refers to the production of practical inventions or useful results.</note>. It is fertile in controversies, but barren of works. 

Indeed, the fable of Scylla <note>In Greek mythology, Scylla was a beautiful nymph transformed into a monster with barking dogs growing from her waist.</note> seems to fit the current state of learning perfectly; she showed the face and features of a virgin, but barking monsters were girt about her womb and clung to it. So too the Sciences we are used to have certain flattering and attractive generalities; but when one comes to the particulars—as if to the organs of generation, so that they might produce fruit and works—then contentions and barking disputes arise. These disputes are the only "offspring" these sciences produce, and they take the place of actual, useful results.

<summary>In this preface, Francis Bacon argues that current scientific knowledge is repetitive and practically useless, comparing Greek-derived philosophy to a child that talks much but produces nothing.</summary>
<keywords>Francis Bacon, Philosophy of Science, Greek Philosophy, Scholasticism, Scylla, Scientific Method, Utility</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the Preface of Francis Bacon's Great Instauration (Instauratio Magna). The text begins mid-word ("nent"), likely concluding a verb from the previous page such as "pertinent" (pertain to) or "continent" (contain).</meta>

-># PREFACE<-

...[pertain to]. Furthermore, if sciences of this kind were not plainly dead things, it seems quite unlikely that what has happened for many centuries now would have occurred: that they remain stuck almost in their own tracks, without taking on growth worthy of the human race. This has reached such a point that frequently not only does an assertion remain a mere assertion, but even a question remains a question; it is not resolved through debate, but rather becomes fixed and fueled by it. 

The entire tradition and succession of these disciplines presents only the roles of Master and Pupil, rather than that of the **Inventor**, or of one who adds something remarkable to what has already been discovered. In the <term>mechanical arts</term> <note>Bacon uses this term to describe practical crafts and technologies—such as printing or masonry—which he contrasts with the stagnant academic philosophy of his time.</note>, however, we see the opposite happening. These, as if they shared in some breath of life, grow and are perfected daily. At their beginning, under their first authors, they usually appear crude, burdensome, and shapeless; but later they acquire new qualities and a certain usefulness, to the point that human interest and desire often fade or change before these arts have even reached their peak of perfection. 

Philosophy and the intellectual sciences, by contrast, are worshipped and celebrated like statues, but they are never moved forward. In fact, they sometimes flourish most under their original author and thereafter decline. For once men have surrendered themselves and devoted themselves to the opinion of a single person (like <term>pedary senators</term> <note>original Latin: "pedarii Senatores." In the Roman Senate, these were lower-ranking members who were not permitted to give speeches but could only vote by walking to one side of the room or the other to indicate their choice.</note>)...

<summary>Bacon argues that while practical crafts (mechanical arts) evolve and improve over time, academic philosophy remains stagnant, acting as a fixed tradition between teachers and students rather than a field of active discovery.</summary>

<meta>This page continues a discussion on the stagnation of the sciences, likely from the preface to Francis Bacon’s "Great Instauration" or "Novum Organum." It follows a critique of how students merely follow old masters rather than expanding knowledge.</meta>

->PREFACE.<-

...[followers] have come together, they do not add breadth to the Sciences themselves, but perform a servile duty in decorating and surrounding certain authors. Nor should anyone suggest that the Sciences, growing little by little, finally reached a certain state, and only then (as if having finished their lawful laps <note>original: "confectis spatiis legitimis" — a metaphor from the racetrack, suggesting the sciences had completed their designated course</note>) took up fixed residences in the works of a few; and that once nothing better could be found, it remained only for what had been discovered to be adorned and cultivated. And it would indeed be desirable if this were the case. 

But it is more correct and truer to say that these <term>enslavements</term> <note>Latin: "mancipationes" — a legal term for the formal transfer of property, suggesting knowledge has been "sold" into the ownership of a few thinkers.</note> of the Sciences are nothing other than a thing born from the confidence of a few men and the sloth and laziness of the rest. For after the Sciences had perhaps been diligently cultivated and handled in parts, then by chance someone arose, bold in talent and popular for the sake of his "Shortcuts of Method" <note>Referring to the tendency of philosophers to create simplified systems that look complete but discourage deeper investigation.</note>, who established an Art in outward appearance, but in reality corrupted the labors of the ancients. 

Yet this is usually pleasing to those who come after, because the work is easy to use, and because of the boredom and impatience associated with new inquiry. If anyone is moved by long-standing consensus, as if it were the judgment of Time, let him know that he relies on a very deceptive and weak reasoning. For it is not largely known to us what has become known in the Sciences and Arts across various ages and places, and what has [flowed out] into the public...

<meta>This page continues the author's introductory critique of the current state of human knowledge, likely from Francis Bacon’s "Great Instauration" or "Novum Organum." It follows a discussion on the origins of scientific errors.</meta>

->**PREFACE**<-

...has flowed out; much less what has been attempted by individuals and debated in secret. Therefore, neither the **Births of Time** nor the **Miscarriages** exist in the public records. <note>original: "Temporis Partus, nec Abortus." Bacon often referred to his early work as "The Masculine Birth of Time." Here he laments that the history of science does not record the failed attempts or private breakthroughs that led to our current knowledge.</note> Neither consensus itself, nor its long duration, should be held in high esteem. For however varied the types of governments may be, the state of the Sciences is singular; it has always been and will remain <term>popular</term> <note>original: "popularis" — in this context, meaning "appealing to the common crowd" or based on superficial, widely-held opinions rather than rigorous evidence.</note>. Among the common people, those doctrines flourish most which are either contentious and pugnacious, or showy and empty; the kind, evidently, that either ensnare or soothe one’s agreement. Therefore, the greatest minds in every age have undoubtedly suffered violence; while men of uncommon grasp and intellect—nonetheless looking out for their own reputation—submitted themselves to the judgment of time and the multitude. Wherefore deeper contemplations, if by chance they ever shone forth, were immediately tossed by the winds of common opinions and extinguished. So much so that **Time**, like a **river**, has carried down to us what is light and inflated, while sinking what is heavy and solid. <note>This is one of Bacon's most famous metaphors: he argues that history is not a filter for quality; instead, the "heavy" (profound and scientific) truths have been lost to history, while "light" (superficial and popular) ideas have floated down to the present day.</note> Moreover, even those authors who assumed a kind of <term>dictatorship</term> <note>original: "dictaturam" — referring to the absolute authority held by ancient philosophers like Aristotle over the academic world.</note> in the Sciences, and pronounce on things with such confidence; yet when they return to themselves at intervals, they turn to complaints about the subtlety of Nature, the hiding places of truth, the obscurity of things, the entanglement of causes, and the weakness of the human mind. In this, they are nonetheless not more modest, since they prefer...

--- Page 14 ---
<meta>This page continues the Preface (Præfatio) of Francis Bacon's *Instauratio Magna* (The Great Instauration), where he critiques the stagnant state of the sciences and the tendency of scholars to rely on ancient authority rather than new discovery.</meta>

-># PREFACE<-

...they <note>The OCR "lint" is a fragment of "velint," meaning "they wish" or "they prefer."</note> prefer to blame the common condition of humanity and nature rather than confess the truth about themselves. Indeed, it is almost a ritual with them that whatever any Art <note>In this context, "Art" refers to a systematic branch of knowledge or a practical skill, such as medicine or logic, rather than the "fine arts."</note> cannot reach, they declare that very thing to be impossible for that art to achieve. Nor can an Art truly be condemned when it is the one doing the debating and the judging. Thus, the goal of these thinkers is merely to ensure that their own ignorance is protected from shame. 

The things that have been handed down to us and accepted are, for the most part, in this state: as far as practical works go, they are sterile and full of endless questions; they are slow and sluggish in their growth; they pretend to be perfect as a whole, but are poorly filled out in their individual parts. Furthermore, they are popular in their choice of topics but are held in suspicion even by their own authors, and are therefore fortified and put on display with certain clever tricks <note>original: "artificiis," implying technical or rhetorical sleights of hand used to make a system seem more complete than it is.</note>. 

Even those who have decided to experiment for themselves and devote themselves to the Sciences <term>Sciences: from the Latin "scientia," meaning organized knowledge or certain understanding</term> in order to extend their boundaries, have neither dared to depart entirely from the accepted traditions nor to seek the actual sources of things. Instead, they think they have achieved something Great if they contribute and add some small thing of their own; prudently considering that they can maintain their modesty by agreeing with the past, while exercising their liberty by adding to it. 

But while these scholars cater to popular opinions and customs, these praised "middle-ways" result in the great detriment of the Sciences. For it is hardly possible to both admire an author and surpass him at the same time. It happens just like water, which never rises higher than the point from which it first descended. Therefore, men of this sort may amend things, but they do not—
<margin>non-</margin>

<summary>Bacon argues that the stagnation of science stems from scholars who blame nature for their own failures and who refuse to move beyond the authority of ancient authors. He compares the current state of knowledge to water that cannot rise above its source, suggesting that true progress requires seeking new "springs" of information.</summary>

--- Page 15 ---
<meta>This page continues the Preface of Francis Bacon's work (likely the *Instauratio Magna* or *Novum Organum*), where he critiques the current state of science and philosophy. He is moving from a general critique of stagnant knowledge to a specific critique of different types of flawed investigators.</meta>

->P R E F A C E.<-

...some few things, but they promote little; they improve things in quality, but not in scope. Nor yet have there been wanting those who, with greater daring, took it upon themselves to handle everything as a whole. Using the force of their own genius, they overthrew and destroyed all that went before to make a way for themselves and their own <term>opinions<note>original Latin: "placitis." This refers to settled dogmas or philosophical decrees that were accepted without proof.</note></term>. From their commotion, however, no great progress was made; they strove not to enlarge Philosophy and the Arts in reality and through practical work, but only to exchange one set of theories for another, seeking to transfer the "kingdom of opinions" to themselves. This yielded very little fruit indeed, since among opposite errors, the causes of straying are almost always the same.

If there were any, however, who were not bound to the opinions of others or even their own, but favored liberty and were so minded that they desired others to join them in their search, their intentions were certainly honorable, but their efforts were weak. They seem to have followed only "probable" reasons and were whirled around by the dizziness of their own arguments. By allowing themselves a wandering freedom in their search, they sapped the rigor of true investigation. 

But no one is found who has spent a proper and lawful amount of time among the actual things of the world and in direct experience. Furthermore, some who have committed themselves to the "waves of experience" have become little more than <term>Mechanics<note>Bacon uses "Mechanics" here to describe artisans or experimentalists who work by trial and error or manual labor without a systematic, scientific theory to guide them.</note></term>. Yet even they conduct a kind of wandering inquiry in that experience, rather than serving under a fixed law. Indeed, most have set themselves only petty tasks, thinking it a great achievement if they can unearth some single discovery; with a plan that is not...

...no less feeble than unskillful. For no one can correctly or successfully investigate the nature of a thing within the thing itself; rather, after a wearying variety of experiments, one does not rest, but simply finds something further to seek.

Nor should we especially overlook this point: that all the industry spent on experimenting has, from the very beginning, chased after certain specific results with over-hasty and untimely zeal. It has sought, I say, <term>Fruit-bearing Experiments</term> <note>original: "Experimenta Fructifera"; these are experiments designed to produce immediate practical or commercial benefits</note> rather than <term>Light-bearing Experiments</term> <note>original: "Experimenta Lucifera"; these are experiments meant to reveal the underlying laws of nature, which Bacon believed should come before practical applications</note>. It has not followed the divine order, which on the first day created light alone, devoting an entire day to it without producing any material work, only descending to such tangible creations on the following days.

Furthermore, those who have assigned the highest importance to <term>Logic</term> <note>original: "Dialecticæ"; referring to the traditional Aristotelian logic taught in universities at the time</note>, and believed that the most reliable defenses for the sciences could be built upon it, saw quite rightly and clearly that the human intellect, when left to its own devices, ought to be held in suspicion. However, the remedy they provided is far weaker than the disease, and is itself not free from the sickness. For while the accepted Logic is perfectly well-suited for civil matters and the arts—which rely on speech and opinion—it falls far short of the subtlety of Nature. By clutching at what it cannot grasp, it has served more to solidify and almost "fix" errors in place than to open a path to the truth.

First: The Divisions of the Sciences.

### 4 THE DISTRIBUTION

...of the understanding, and that its power might be expanded to overcome the hardships and obscurities of Nature. This method which we introduce—which we have made it a habit to call the ***Interpretation of Nature***—is a form of Logic; yet the difference between our method and the common version is vast, even immeasurable. To be sure, ordinary Logic also claims to construct and provide aids and protections for the Understanding; in this single point, they agree. However, our method differs fundamentally from the common version in three main areas: specifically, in its ultimate goal, in the sequence of proof, and in the starting points of the inquiry.

   For the goal proposed for this Science of ours is the discovery not of arguments, but of arts; not of things that merely fit with established principles, but the very principles themselves; and not of probable reasons, but of the blueprints and directions for practical Works <note>original: "Opere". Bacon emphasizes that "Works"—the ability to create or change things in the physical world—is the true test of knowledge.</note>. Because the intention is different, a different result follows. In the old logic, an opponent is defeated and bound by Disputation; in ours, Nature is defeated by Work.

   The nature and order of the proofs themselves must align with this goal. In common Logic, almost all effort is spent on the **Syllogism** <term>Syllogism: A traditional form of logical argument where a conclusion is drawn from two premises (e.g., All men are mortal; Socrates is a man; therefore Socrates is mortal).</term>. Concerning **Induction** <term>Induction: A method of reasoning that moves from specific observations to broader generalizations; Bacon believes this is the only way to truly understand nature.</term>, the teachers of logic seem to have hardly given it a serious thought, passing over it with a brief mention while hurrying toward their formulas for debating. But we reject proof by Syllogism because it operates too confusedly and lets Nature slip through its fingers. For while no one can doubt that things which agree in a **middle term** <term>Middle Term: The connecting link between two ideas in a formal logic argument.</term> also agree with each other (which...

<summary>Francis Bacon explains how his "Interpretation of Nature" differs from traditional logic by focusing on practical discovery and the "Induction" method rather than verbal debate and "Syllogisms." He argues that true science should aim to master nature through work and experimentation rather than simply winning arguments.</summary>

<keywords>Interpretation of Nature, Logic, Syllogism, Induction, Scientific Method, Disputation, Principles, Francis Bacon</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Francis Bacon's "Plan of the Work" (Distributio Operis) from his Great Instauration. In the preceding section, he began discussing the flaws in traditional logic and the need for a new method of inquiry.</meta>

->OF THE WORK. 5<-

(which is of a certain mathematical certainty): nevertheless, there is a deception lurking beneath this, in that the <term>Syllogism<note>A form of logical argument where a conclusion is drawn from two shared premises (e.g., All men are mortal; Socrates is a man; therefore Socrates is mortal). Bacon argues this is useless if the words used are poorly defined.</note></term> consists of propositions, propositions consist of words, and words are the tokens and signs of notions. Therefore, if the **Notions** of the mind themselves (which are, as it were, the soul of words and the basis of this whole structural fabric) are poorly and rashly abstracted from things, and are vague or not sufficiently defined and circumscribed—in short, if they are faulty in many ways—then everything collapses. 

We therefore reject the Syllogism; and not only regarding first principles (to which even the traditionalists do not apply it), but also regarding the intermediate propositions. The Syllogism does indeed draw out and give birth to these in some fashion, but they are barren of results, remote from practical application, and clearly incompetent regarding the active branch of the Sciences. Although we leave to the Syllogism and similar famous and celebrated forms of demonstration their jurisdiction over the popular arts and matters of opinion (for we do not wish to interfere there), nevertheless, when dealing with the **Nature of Things**, we employ **Induction** through and through, for both the minor and major propositions. 

*For we consider Induction to be that form of demonstration which protects the senses, stays close to Nature, and bears upon—almost merging with—practical works.*

Thus, the order of demonstration is also completely inverted. For until now, it has been the custom to proceed from the senses and particulars, in the first place...

<summary>Bacon critiques the syllogism as a tool for science, arguing that it relies on poorly defined words and concepts. He proposes a new reliance on "Induction" as a method that remains grounded in sensory observation and practical application.</summary>

...one flies to the most general <term>Axioms: In Bacon’s context, these are general scientific principles or laws derived from observation, rather than just self-evident logical truths.</term>, as if to fixed poles around which disputations turn; from those, the rest are derived through intermediate steps. These most general principles turn out not to be mere abstract notions, but well-defined; they are the kind of truths that Nature recognizes as truly "better known to herself," and which stick in the very marrow of things.

But in the very form of **Induction** itself, and the judgment made through it, we propose a work of the greatest importance. For the kind of induction the <note>original: "Dialectici". Bacon is referring to the Logicians of his time who followed traditional Aristotelian methods.</note> Logicians speak of—which proceeds by **simple enumeration**—is a childish thing; it concludes precariously, is exposed to the danger of a contradictory instance, and looks only at common, obvious things; it finds no successful outcome.

Yet for the Sciences, we need a form of Induction that analyzes and separates experience, and arrives at a necessary conclusion through proper exclusions and rejections <note>Bacon’s "method of exclusions" is a process of elimination used to find the true cause of a phenomenon by ruling out what is not responsible.</note>. If that common "Judgment" of the Logicians was so laborious and occupied such great minds, how much more must we labor on this other kind, which is extracted not only from the inner chambers of the Mind, but even from the very bowels of Nature!

Nor is this the end. For the foundations...

->OF THE WORK. 9<-

We are preparing the introduction: things which might be sufficient in themselves if the human Intellect were equitable and like a <term>smoothed tablet</term> <note>original: *tabula rasa*; the philosophical concept of the mind as a blank slate before experience writes upon it.</note>. But since the minds of men are preoccupied in strange ways—so that a clear and polished surface is entirely lacking for receiving the true rays of Things—a certain necessity is imposed upon us, so that we believe a remedy must also be sought for this matter.

Now the *Idols* <note>original: *Idola*; Bacon’s term for the various illusions, prejudices, and fallacies that distort human understanding.</note> by which the Mind is occupied are either acquired or Innate. The acquired ones have migrated into the minds of men either from the doctrines and sects of Philosophers, or from perverse laws of demonstration. But the Innate ones are inherent to the very Nature of the Intellect itself, which is found to be far more prone to error than the Senses. For however much men may please themselves, and rush into admiration and almost adoration of the human Mind, this much is certain: just as an uneven mirror changes the rays of objects by its own shape and cross-section, so also the mind—when it is affected by things through the Senses—does not act with the best faith in developing and devising its notions, but rather inserts and mingles its own nature with the nature of Things.

And those first two types of *Idols* are removed with difficulty; but these latter ones <note>referring to the Innate Idols</note> can be uprooted in no way at all. All that remains is that they be pointed out, and that this treacherous power of the Mind be noted and proven guilty; lest perhaps, after the destruction of the old errors, new shoots of error might continually sprout up from the very bad complexion of the Mind: and that—

->OF THE WORK. 11<-

But for those who intend not to guess and <note>original: "hariolari" — to act as a soothsayer or divine, implying guesswork rather than science.</note> play the prophet, but to discover and know; and who have it in mind not to devise <note>original: "simiolas" — little apes or mimicries. For up to this very day, the affairs of men have been conducted in such a way that it is no wonder if Nature does not grant access to herself.

For first, the information of the sense itself is both failing and deceptive; Observation is careless, uneven, and as if by chance; Tradition is vain and based on rumor; Practice is focused narrowly on the task and is servile; Experimental power is blind, dull, wandering, and abrupt; finally, Natural History, being shallow and poor, has piled up the most defective material for the Intellect to use for Philosophy and the Sciences.

Then, the backward subtlety and winnowing of Argument is attempted as a late remedy for matters that are clearly desperate; it does not restore the business in any way, nor does it separate out errors. Therefore, no hope of greater increase and progress lies, except in a certain <term>Restoration of the Sciences</term> <note>Bacon's famous "Instauratio," his project to rebuild human knowledge from the ground up through empirical observation rather than relying on ancient authorities.</note>.

->12      DISTRIBUTION<-

The beginnings of this undertaking must be taken entirely from natural history, and a history of a completely new kind and composition. For it would be in vain to polish the mirror <note>Bacon frequently uses the metaphor of the mind as a mirror that needs to be cleaned of "idols" or distortions to reflect the light of nature accurately.</note> if the images themselves are missing; and clearly, suitable material must be prepared for the **Intellect**, not just reliable aids provided to it. Moreover, our History differs (just as our Logic does) from the kind currently in use in many respects: in its end or purpose; in its very scale and collection; then in its precision; and also in its selection and arrangement in relation to the stages that follow.

For first, we propose a **Natural History** that does not so much delight with a variety of things, or provide help through the immediate fruit of experiments, but rather sheds light upon the discovery of causes and offers the first breast to nourish Philosophy. For although we chiefly pursue **Works** <note>original: "Opera" — Bacon refers to practical, "active" results and technologies rather than just theoretical knowledge.</note> and the active part of the sciences, we nevertheless wait for the time of harvest, and do not try to reap the moss and the green crop before they are ready. For we know well enough that rightly discovered <term>Axioms: General principles or laws of nature derived from systematic observation.</term> draw whole troops of **Works** along with them, and display those works not sparingly, but in great abundance. We utterly condemn and reject that untimely and childish desire to hastily snatch up some small pledges of new **Works**, as if they were the apple of Atalanta <note>In Greek mythology, the swift runner Atalanta was distracted from her race by golden apples thrown to tempt her; Bacon uses this to warn against being distracted from the pursuit of truth by the lure of immediate, minor practical gains.</note> which slows down the race. Such is the duty of our Natural History.

->OF THE WORK. 13<-

Regarding the collection <note>original: *congeriem*—referring to the vast gathering of observations and data required for his new scientific method</note> of materials, we are composing a history not only of nature free and unconstrained (when, of course, she flows of her own accord and performs her own work; such as the history of the Heavens, Meteors, the Earth and Sea, Minerals, Plants, and Animals); but much more of nature constrained and vexed <note>This is one of Bacon’s most famous concepts: the idea that nature reveals her secret mechanics more clearly when "vexed" or "teased" by experimental intervention than when left alone</note>; namely, when through <term>Art|the application of human skill, technology, or craft</term> and human ministry she is forced out of her natural state, pressed, and molded. Therefore, we record all experiments of the Mechanical Arts, all those from the operative <note>The "working" or practical application, as opposed to the purely theoretical</note> part of the Liberal Arts, and those from various practical skills which have not yet developed into a formal "art" (as far as we have been able to investigate and as far as they serve our purpose). Moreover (to speak plainly), having no regard for human pride or outward appearances, we devote much more effort and support to this part of the work than the other; since the nature of things reveals itself more clearly under the trials of <term>Art|experimental science</term> than in its own natural freedom.

Nor do we present a history of bodies alone; rather, we have considered it a duty of our diligence to also prepare a separate history of the <term>Virtues|the fundamental powers, capacities, or properties of matter</term> themselves. We refer to those which might be considered "Cardinal" <note>From the Latin *cardo* (hinge); the fundamental properties upon which the rest of nature turns</note> in Nature, and in which the very foundations of Nature are established; specifically Matter and its primary <term>Passions|the ways in which matter is acted upon or its inherent tendencies</term> and desires; namely: the Dense, the Rare, the Hot, the Cold, the Solid, the Fluid, the Heavy, the Light, and many others besides.

14      THE PLAN <note>original: "DISTRIBUTIO". This section outlines the structure of Bacon's ambitious project to reform all human knowledge.</note>

Indeed, to speak of Subtlety, we clearly seek out a kind of experiment far more subtle and simple than those which commonly occur. It is thus clearly apparent that these things were not sought for their own sake; but they stand in relation to Things and Works exactly as the letters of the Alphabet stand to Speech and words; which, though useless by themselves, are nonetheless the elements of all discourse. <note>Bacon argues that "useless" basic research is the "alphabet" required to eventually write the "words" of practical technology.</note>

->OF THE WORK. 15<-

From the Greek *akatalēpsia*, meaning "impossibility of comprehension." Bacon is referring to the Ancient Greek Skeptics who argued that nothing can be known with certainty.</note></term> were not inferior to those who took the liberty of making dogmatic pronouncements. Yet those former schools provided no aids to the Senses and the Intellect, as we have done; instead, they completely did away with all trust and authority, which is a very different thing, and almost its opposite.

    The sixth and final part of our Work (to which all the other parts serve and minister) at last reveals and proposes that Philosophy which is drawn out and built from a legitimate, pure, and rigorous inquiry—the kind we have previously taught and prepared. However, to complete this final Part and bring it to its conclusion is a task that lies both beyond our individual strength and beyond our hopes. We provide for it (as we hope) beginnings that are not to be despised; the future fortune of the human race will provide the conclusion—one that perhaps men, in their current state of affairs and mind, cannot easily grasp or measure. For it is not only a matter of **Contemplative happiness** <note>Bacon refers here to the traditional Aristotelian ideal that the highest good is pure study or "thinking about thinking."</note> that is at stake, but truly the welfare and fortune of humanity, and the entire power of our Works. For man, the servant and interpreter of Nature, only performs and understands as much as he has observed of the order, work, or mind of Nature; he knows no more, and can do no more. For no forces are able to loosen or break the chain of Causes; nor is Nature conquered in any other way than by obeying her. <note>The text ends with the word "vinci-," the beginning of "vincitur" (conquered), which is completed on the following page.</note>

<summary>Bacon describes the sixth part of his project—a new philosophy based on rigorous evidence—and argues that human power over nature is only possible through understanding and obeying natural laws.</summary>

-> OF THE WORK. 19 <-

...is conquered. Therefore, those twin goals, namely human *Knowledge* and *Power*, truly meet in the same point: and the failure of Works <note>Bacon uses "Works" to mean practical inventions or successful applications of science</note> arises chiefly from the ignorance of Causes.

And everything depends on this: that one never turns the eyes of the Mind away from things themselves, but receives their images exactly as they are. For God forbid that we should publish a dream of our own Imagination as a Model of the World: but rather may He graciously grant that we may write a Revelation <note>original: "Apocalypsim," used here in the sense of an "unveiling" of nature's secrets</note> and a true vision of the footprints and seals of the Creator impressed upon His creatures.

Therefore You, *Father*, who gave visible light as the first-fruits of Creation, and breathed Intellectual light into the face of Man as the pinnacle of your Works; protect and guide this Work, which, having come forth from your Goodness, seeks your glory. After You turned to look at the Works which your hands had made, You saw that all were very good; and You rested. But Man, when he turned to the Works which his own hands had made, saw that all were vanity and vexation of spirit; nor did he find any rest. Therefore, if we labor <note>literally "sweat"</note> in your Works, You will make us partakers of your vision and of your Sabbath <note>A reference to the divine rest after the six days of creation; Bacon suggests that true scientific discovery leads to a similar holy peace</note>. We humbly pray that this purpose may remain firm in us: and that through new Alms <note>Bacon views scientific discoveries as "alms" or charitable gifts to benefit the human race</note> by our hands and the hands of others to whom You grant the same mind, You would be pleased to enrich the human family.

## THE NEW ORGANON, OR <note>original: "Novum Organum." The title suggests a "New Tool" or "New Instrument," intended to replace Aristotle's "Organon" (his works on logic).</note>
## TRUE DIRECTIONS CONCERNING THE INTERPRETATION OF NATURE.

### PREFACE.

**Q**ui who have dared to pronounce on Nature as if it were a subject already thoroughly explored—whether they did so out of personal confidence or ambitiously and in a professional manner—have brought the greatest harm to Philosophy and the Sciences. For while they were powerful in gaining credit for their ideas, they were equally effective at extinguishing and cutting off further inquiry. Nor did they do as much good by their own ability as they did harm in this: they corrupted and destroyed the ability of others.

But those who have entered upon the opposite path and asserted that nothing at all can be known—whether they did so from the ancient Sophists... <note>Bacon is contrasting two extremes: the "Dogmatists" who think they know everything, and the "Skeptics" who believe knowledge is impossible. ...from a hatred of the past, or from a wavering of the mind, or even from a certain abundance of learning, have fallen into this opinion, they have certainly brought forward arguments for it that are not to be despised; nevertheless, they did not derive their opinion from true starting points, and through a certain zeal and affectation, they have utterly exceeded all bounds. Our method, however, while difficult in execution, is easy to describe. ...attributed. From this it is clear that they sought aids for the *Intellect*, but held the *Mind’s* natural and spontaneous process in suspicion. Truly, if men had attempted *Mechanical* works with their bare hands, without the power and help of tools, just as they have not hesitated to handle *Intellectual* works with almost the bare powers of the *Mind*; the things they could have moved and overcome would have been very small indeed, even if they had put forth strenuous and even collective efforts. ...of madness, would any sober spectator of the matter not admit it? <meta>This page continues Francis Bacon's preface to his work on the new scientific method. Having previously discussed the errors of past philosophy, he now addresses how he intends to present his own work without appearing to disrespect the great thinkers of antiquity.</meta>

We wish to give a clear warning, lest these points perhaps escape the readers’ notice or pass them by. The first of these is as follows: it happens by a certain good fate (as we believe), for the sake of extinguishing and driving away contradictions and the restless rumors of minds, so that the honor and reverence due to the **Ancients** <note>Bacon refers to the classical Greek and Roman philosophers, such as Aristotle and Plato, who had dominated European thought for centuries.</note> may remain untouched and undiminished, while we may complete our intended goals and yet reap the fruit of our own modesty. 

For if we were to claim that we bring better things than the ancients while following the same path as they did, no skill of words could prevent a comparison—or rather a competition—of **talent**, **excellence**, or **ability** <term>facultas: a person's inherent capability or mental power</term> from being introduced. Such a competition would not be unlawful or new; after all, why shouldn't we be able, by our own right (a right shared by everyone), to criticize or point out anything that was not correctly discovered or established by them? However, no matter how just or permitted such a challenge might be, that very competition would perhaps have been an unequal match, given the limit of our own strengths. 

But since our purpose is to open an entirely different path for the **Intellect**, one untried and unknown to them, the situation is now changed. Rivalry and partisanship <note>original: "studium & partes," referring to the tendency of scholars to form "camps" or "sects" around specific ideologies.</note> cease to exist. We take on only the role of a **guide** <note>original: "indicis," one who points the way or acts as a signpost rather than a master teacher.</note>; a role which certainly carries modest authority, and is a matter of a certain good fortune rather than of personal ability and excellence. And this type of warning pertains to **Persons**; the other pertains to the **Things** themselves.

<summary>Bacon explains that he is not competing with Ancient philosophers on their own terms, but is instead proposing an entirely new path for human understanding. ### VII.

**The productions** of the Mind and the Hand appear quite numerous in books and manufactures. But all that variety consists in the extreme <term>subtlety<note>Bacon uses "subtlety" (Latin: *subtilitas*) to describe the intricate, fine-grained complexity of the natural world that often escapes human perception.</note></term> and the derivations of a few things that have already become known; it does not come from a great number of <term>Axioms<note>In this context, "axioms" are the general principles or laws of nature that should be the foundation of scientific knowledge.</note></term>.

### VIII.

**Even the Works** which have already been discovered are owed to chance and experience, more than to the sciences. For the sciences we now possess are nothing more than certain arrangements of things previously discovered; they are not methods of discovery or blueprints for new Works.

### IX.

**The cause** and root of nearly all evils in the sciences is this one: that while we falsely admire and extol the powers of the human mind, we do not seek its true aids.

### X.

**The subtlety** of Nature surpasses the subtlety of the Senses and the Intellect many times over; so that those beautiful meditations, and human speculations...

### XI.

**Just as** the Sciences which we now possess are useless for the discovery of **Works** <note>Bacon uses "Works" (Operum) to mean practical inventions and applications that improve the human condition.</note>: So also the **Logic** which we now possess is useless for the discovery of **Sciences**.

### XII.

**Logic**, as it is currently misused, serves to stabilize and fix errors (which are founded on common notions) rather than to assist in the search for truth; so that it is more harmful than useful.

### XIII.

The **Syllogism** <term>Syllogism: A traditional form of logical argument where a conclusion is drawn from two premises (e.g., All men are mortal; Socrates is a man; therefore Socrates is mortal).</term> is not applied to the first Principles of the Sciences; it is applied in vain to intermediate axioms, since it is far from equal to the subtlety of Nature. It therefore constrains our **assent** <note>original: "Assensum"; meaning the logical agreement of the mind.</note>, but not the **things** themselves <note>Bacon argues that while a logical argument might be "valid" on paper, it does not actually capture or control the physical reality of nature.</note>.

### XIV.

The **Syllogism** consists of Propositions, propositions consist of words, and words are the tokens <note>original: "tesserae"; symbols or counters used for identification.</note> of **Notions**. Therefore, if the notions themselves (which are the very basis of the matter) are confused and recklessly abstracted from things, there is no firmness in anything built upon them.

<summary>Francis Bacon argues that traditional Aristotelian logic and the syllogism are ineffective for scientific discovery because they rely on poorly defined words and concepts rather than a direct, accurate observation of nature.</summary>

### XV.
In our notions <note>Bacon uses "notions" to mean the basic concepts or categories we use to understand the world</note> there is nothing sound, neither in Logic nor in Physics. Neither *Substance*, nor *Quality*, *Action*, *Passion*, nor *Being* itself, are sound notions; much less are *Heavy*, *Light*, *Dense*, *Rare* <note>Latin: *tenue*, referring to the thinness or lack of density in a substance</note>, *Moist*, *Dry*, *Generation*, *Corruption* <note>In the Aristotelian tradition, "generation" is coming into existence and "corruption" is the process of decaying or ceasing to be</note>, *Attraction*, *Repulsion*, *Element*, *Matter*, *Form*, and that sort; rather, all are fantastical and ill-defined.

### XVI.
The notions of the lowest species <note>The most specific classifications, like individual types of animals</note>, such as *Man*, *Dog*, *Dove*, and the immediate perceptions of the senses, such as *Hot*, *Cold*, *White*, and *Black*, do not deceive us much; yet even these are sometimes confused by the flux of matter and the mixing of things. All other notions (which men have used until now) are aberrations, being neither abstracted nor derived from things by the proper methods.

### XVII.
Nor is there less caprice and wandering in the establishing of <term>Axioms</term> <note>General principles or scientific laws</note> than in the abstracting of notions; and this is especially true of the primary principles, which depend on common <term>induction</term> <note>The traditional method of drawing a general rule from a few specific examples</note>. However, the error is much less in the lower axioms and propositions which the <term>syllogism</term> <note>A form of deductive reasoning where a conclusion is reached from two given premises</note> produces.

->B 4<- ### XVIII.

<summary>Bacon argues that the basic concepts and scientific laws of his time are poorly defined and unreliably formed, though specific sensory observations and deductive logic are slightly less prone to error than broad generalizations.</summary>

<keywords>notions, axioms, Aristotelian physics, induction, syllogism, scientific method, critique of logic</keywords>

### XVIII.

The discoveries that have been made in the sciences up to this point are of such a kind that they remain subject to common notions <note>original: "notionibus vulgaribus"; Bacon refers to everyday, unexamined ideas that lack scientific rigour</note>. However, to penetrate the inner and more remote parts of Nature, it is necessary that both Notions and Axioms <term>Axioms: In Bacon’s work, these are not self-evident truths but general principles or laws of nature derived from observation.</term> be drawn from things themselves by a more certain and secure path, and that an altogether better and more reliable operation of the Intellect be brought into use.

### XIX.

There are, and can be, only two ways of searching for and discovering truth. One flies from the senses and particulars <note>Specific, individual observations</note> to the most general Axioms, and from those principles—and their supposedly unshakable truth—proceeds to judge and discover "middle axioms." This is the way currently in use. The other way draws Axioms from the senses and particulars by climbing steadily and by degrees, so that it reaches the most general axioms only at the very last; this is the true way, but it is as yet untried.

### XX.

The Intellect, when left to its own devices, enters that same path (the former one) which it follows according to the order of Logic <note>original: "Dialecticæ"; Bacon is critiquing the traditional Aristotelian logic taught in universities</note>. For the Mind longs to leap to more general principles so that it may find a resting place, and after a short while, it becomes weary of experience.

### XXI.
**The intellect**, when left to its own devices in a sober, patient, and serious mind (especially if it is not hindered by received doctrines <note>The "received doctrines" refers to the established philosophical and scientific teachings of the time, particularly those of the Scholastics.</note>), tries to some extent that other way—the right one—but with little progress. For the Intellect, unless it is governed and assisted, is an uneven tool, and entirely unfit to overcome the obscurity of nature.

### XXII.
**Both Ways** begin from the senses and individual facts, and come to rest in the most general principles. However, they differ immensely. One way merely brushes past experience and particulars in a glancing way; the other dwells among them properly and in due Order. Furthermore, the first way establishes certain abstract and useless generalities from the very beginning; the other rises by degrees to those principles which are truly "better known to Nature" <note>original: "Naturæ sunt notiora." This is a reference to the classical distinction between things that are easy for humans to perceive versus the fundamental laws that actually govern the universe.</note>.

### XXIII.
**There is no small difference** between the **Idols** <term>Idols (Idola)</term><note>Bacon's famous concept of "Idols" refers to the various mental biases, errors, and illusions that distort human perception and prevent us from seeing the world as it truly is.</note> of the human mind and the **Ideas** of the divine mind—that is, between certain empty dogmas and the true signatures and impressions made upon created things, exactly as they are found.

### XXIV.

It is in no way possible for <term>Axioms</term> <note>In Bacon's writing, "axioms" are general principles or laws of nature derived from observation.</note> established by mere argument to be useful for the discovery of new works; this is because the subtlety of Nature surpasses the subtlety of argument by many degrees. However, when Axioms are properly and systematically drawn from <term>particulars</term> <note>Specific facts, individual observations, or data points.</note>, they easily point the way toward new particulars in turn. In this way, they make the sciences active and productive.

### XXV.

The Axioms currently in use are derived from thin and meager experience—a mere handful of particulars that occur most frequently. These principles are crafted and stretched just enough to cover those specific cases; thus, it is no surprise if they do not lead us to new discoveries. If, by chance, some new instance arises that was not previously noticed or known, the existing Axiom is usually "saved" by some trivial distinction, when it would be far more truthful to simply amend the principle itself.

### XXVI.

For the sake of teaching, we have become accustomed to calling that common human reasoning we apply to Nature <term>Anticipations of Nature</term> <note>original: "Anticipationes Naturæ." This refers to the human tendency to jump to conclusions before gathering enough evidence.</note> (because it is a rash and premature process). However, that reasoning which is drawn from facts in the proper manner, we call the <term>Interpretation of Nature</term> <note>original: "Interpretationem Naturæ." This is Bacon’s term for his new scientific method.</note>.

### XXVII.

<summary>Bacon argues that true scientific progress requires axioms derived systematically from specific observations rather than mere logic, distinguishing between "Anticipations of Nature" (rash guesses) and "Interpretations of Nature" (true science).</summary>

->XXVII.<-

Anticipations <note>original: "Anticipationes"; Bacon uses this term to describe the premature conclusions or "shortcuts" the mind takes before performing a proper investigation of nature</note> are strong enough to produce consensus; for even if all men went mad in the same way and followed the same fashion, they could still agree with one another well enough.

->XXVIII.<-

Indeed, *Anticipations* are far more powerful at gaining our agreement than *Interpretations*; because they are gathered from only a few instances—and specifically those that occur to us most familiarly—they immediately strike the Intellect and fill the imagination. In contrast, *Interpretations*, which are gathered from things that are widely varied and far apart, cannot strike the Intellect suddenly. Consequently, to common Opinion, these Interpretations must necessarily seem harsh and discordant, almost like the mysteries of faith <note>Bacon suggests that true scientific discoveries often seem "unbelievable" or counter-intuitive to the average person, much like religious dogmas do to the uninitiated</note>.

### XXXIV.

The method for passing on or explaining what we are presenting is not easy. This is because things that are new in themselves will still be interpreted through the lens of old ideas <note>original: *ex analogia veterum*. Bacon is concerned that readers will try to fit his new "Inductive" method into the boxes of old "Aristotelian" logic, thereby misunderstanding it.</note>.

### XXXV.

**Borgia** said of the **French** expedition into **Italy** that they came with chalk in their hands to mark their lodgings, rather than with weapons to break through doors <note>This refers to the 1494 invasion by Charles VIII of France. The campaign was so swift and met with so little resistance that it was joked the King only needed to send harbingers ahead with chalk to mark which houses his soldiers would occupy, rather than having to fight his way in.</note>. Our method is much the same: we want our teaching to slide quietly into minds that are ready and able to receive it. There is no point in using refutations or arguments when we disagree on the very first principles, the basic concepts, and even the forms of logic used in demonstrations.

### XXXVI.

There remains only one simple way for us to communicate: we must lead people to the specific facts of nature <note>original: *particularia*</note>, their sequences, and their patterns. People must, for a time, force themselves to set aside their preconceived notions and begin to familiarize themselves with the things themselves.

### XXXVII.

The reasoning of those who held the doctrine of <term>Acatalepsia|A philosophical position, often associated with the New Academy of ancient Greece, asserting that things are ultimately "un-knowable" or that the human mind cannot attain absolute certainty.</term> and our own path agree somewhat in their beginnings; however, in the end they differ immensely <note>The text cuts off mid-word: *dis-* likely leading to *dissentiunt* (differ/disagree).</note>.

## XLVI.

The human intellect, when it has once adopted an opinion (either because it is a widely accepted belief or because it is pleasing), forces everything else to support and agree with it. Even if there are a greater number and weight of instances to the contrary, the intellect either ignores them, treats them with contempt, or uses technical distinctions to set them aside and reject them. It does this with a great and dangerous prejudice, simply so that the authority of its initial <term>conceptions</term> <note>original: "Syllepsibus" – refers to the way the mind "seizes" or bundles ideas together into a conclusion.</note> remains unchallenged. 

Therefore, he gave a good answer who—when shown a painted tablet in a temple of those who had fulfilled their vows because they survived a shipwreck, and was then pressured to admit the power of the Gods—asked in response: *But where are the pictures of those who drowned after making their vows?* <note>Bacon is likely citing a story about the Greek philosopher Diagoras of Melos or perhaps Cicero’s retelling of a similar anecdote.</note> 

This is the basis of almost all superstition, whether in Astrology, Dreams, Omens, <term>Divine Retributions</term> <note>original: "Nemesibus" – referring to the idea of inevitable poetic justice or divine punishment.</note>, and the like. In these matters, men—delighting in such vanities—notice the events when they come true; but when they fail (which happens much more often), they simply ignore them and look the other way.

### XLVII.

The human intellect is most moved by those things that can strike and enter the mind simultaneously and suddenly; these are the things that typically fill and puff up the imagination. The human intellect is restless; it cannot stop or find rest, but always seeks to go further, though in vain. ...impatience in inquiry; sober things, because they restrict hope; the deeper secrets of Nature, because of superstition; the light of experience, because of arrogance and pride, lest the Mind should seem to be occupied with things mean and fleeting; paradoxes, because of the opinion of the common people; and finally, in countless ways, and sometimes imperceptible ones, the affections <note>original: "affectus"; Bacon refers to the emotions and the will, arguing that our desires color our logic.</note> color and infect the understanding.

### L.

BUT by far the greatest hindrance and distortion of the human understanding arises from the dullness, incompetence, and deceptions of the senses; in that those things which strike the sense outweigh those things which do not strike the sense immediately, even if they are more important. Thus, contemplation generally ends where the sight ends; so much so that there is little or no observation of invisible things. Therefore, every operation of the spirits <note>original: "spirituum"; in 17th-century natural philosophy, "spirits" were considered active, subtle substances or gases trapped within solid matter that governed its behavior.</note> enclosed in tangible bodies lies hidden and escapes notice. Every more subtle transformation <term>metaschematismus: the internal structural arrangement or "schematism" of the minute parts of a body</term> in the parts of solid things (which is commonly called "alteration," though it is actually a motion through the smallest particles) remains likewise hidden; and yet, unless these two things which we have mentioned are explored and brought to light, nothing great can be achieved in Nature regarding practical works. Again, the very nature of common air, and of all bodies that surpass air in thinness (of which there are many), is almost unknown. For the sense by itself is a weak and wandering thing; nor do instruments...

**LI.**

The human intellect is drawn toward abstractions due to its own nature: and those things which are in flux, it imagines to be constant. It is better, however, to dissect <note>The original Latin *secare* implies a physical or anatomical cutting, suggesting we should look at the "machinery" of nature rather than theorizing about its "essence."</note> Nature than to abstract her; this is what the school of *Democritus* <note>Democritus was an ancient Greek philosopher famous for the "atomist" theory, which Bacon preferred over the more abstract theories of Plato or Aristotle.</note> did, which penetrated more deeply into Nature than the rest. We should consider matter instead, along with its configurations <term>Schematisms: the internal structures or arrangements of parts within a body</term> and its changes of configuration <term>Metaschematisms: the transformation or restructuring of those internal parts</term>, as well as pure act and the law of action, or Motion. For "Forms" <note>Bacon is dismissing the traditional Scholastic idea of "Forms" as abstract, mystical blueprints of things.</note> are mere figments of the human mind, unless one prefers to call those laws of action "Forms."

**LII.**

Such, then, are the Idols which we call the *Idols of the Tribe* <note>original: *Idola Tribus*</note>; which arise either from the uniform nature of the human spirit; or its prejudices; or its limitations; or its restless motion; or the influence of the passions; or the failure of the Senses; or the manner in which impressions are received.

**LIII.**

LIII.

The **Idols of the Cave** <note>Latin: *Idola Specus*. Bacon uses the word "Idol" to mean a false mental image or a prejudice that clouds our judgment. The "Cave" refers to Plato's famous allegory, suggesting each person lives in their own private cavern of distorted perception.</note> have their origin in the particular nature of each individual’s soul and body; and also from education, habit, and chance occurrences. Although this category is varied and manifold, we shall nevertheless set forth those things which require the greatest caution, and which have the most power to pollute the understanding so that it is no longer pure.

LIV.

Men become attached to particular sciences and contemplations; either because they believe themselves to be the authors and inventors of them, or because they have put the most effort into them and have become most accustomed to them. Indeed, if men of this kind turn themselves toward philosophy and universal contemplations, they twist and corrupt them according to their prior fantasies <note>Bacon uses "fantasies" here to mean preconceived notions or fixed ideas that color one's entire worldview.</note>. This is seen most clearly in *Aristotle*, who completely enslaved his natural philosophy to his logic, so that he rendered it almost useless and full of contention <note>original: *contentiosam*. This refers to the argumentative style of the "Schoolmen" who followed Aristotle, focusing more on winning debates than discovering physical truths.</note>. Moreover, the tribe of chemists <note>This refers to the alchemists of Bacon's time.</note>, from a few experiments at the furnace, have built up a fantastic philosophy of limited scope. Furthermore, *Gilbert* <note>William Gilbert (1544–1603), an English physician and physicist who performed pioneering work on magnetism.</note>, after he had applied himself most laboriously to observations of the magnet, immediately proceeded to construct a whole system of philosophy in accordance with his favorite subject.

<summary>This page defines the "Idols of the Cave"—the personal biases shaped by an individual's background—and criticizes thinkers like Aristotle and Gilbert for forcing all of nature to fit into their specific areas of expertise.</summary>

### LV.

The greatest and, as it were, most fundamental difference between minds, regarding Philosophy and the Sciences, is this: that some minds are stronger and more capable of noticing the **differences** in things, while others are better at noticing the **similarities** in things. For steady and sharp minds are able to fix their contemplations, and linger, and dwell on every subtle point of difference; whereas lofty and discursive <term>discursive: moving rapidly from one thought to another, or reasoning through a wide range of subjects</term> minds recognize and combine even the thinnest and most universal <note>original: "catholicas"</note> similarities between things. Each type of mind, however, easily falls into excess, by grasping at either the minute nuances <note>original: "gradus" – literally steps or degrees</note> of things or their mere shadows.

### LVI.

There are some minds found to be lost in an extreme admiration of **Antiquity**, others in a love and embrace of **Novelty**; yet few are of such a temperament that they can hold a middle ground. They either tear down what was correctly established by the Ancients, or they scorn what is correctly offered by the Moderns. This happens to the great detriment of the sciences and Philosophy, since these tendencies are passions for the Old or the New, rather than balanced judgments. Truth, however, is not to be sought from the good fortune of any particular time—which is a variable thing—but from the light of Nature and Experience, which is eter[nal]— <note>The text cuts off mid-word: "aeterna" (eternal).</note>

### LVII.

Contemplations of Nature and of bodies in their simplicity <note>referring to the basic, individual components or atoms of matter</note> break and crumble the intellect; while contemplations of Nature and of bodies in their composition and configuration <note>the complex way things are built or structured</note> stun and dissolve the intellect. ### LIX.
BUT the *Idols of the Market* <note>original: "Idola Fori." These are errors that arise from the way humans communicate and socialized language.</note> are the most troublesome of all; these have crept into the Intellect through the alliance of words and names. For men believe that their reason governs words. But it also happens that words turn and reflect their power back upon the Intellect, which has rendered Philosophy and the Sciences <term>sophistical</term> <note>In this context, "sophistical" refers to reasoning that is clever in appearance but fallacious or empty of real-world value.</note> and inactive. Words are mostly assigned according to the understanding of the common people, and they divide things along lines most obvious to the common intellect. However, when a sharper Intellect or more diligent observation wants to shift those lines so they are more in accordance with nature, words cry out in protest. Thus it happens that great and solemn disputes among learned men often end in controversies over words and names; it would be wiser (following the custom and prudence of Mathematicians) to begin with these, and bring them into order through definitions. Yet these definitions, in natural and material things, cannot cure this evil; since definitions themselves consist of words, and words beget words: so that it is necessary to return to <term>particular instances</term> <note>Bacon's term for specific, observable facts or experiments in nature.</note>, and their sequences and orders;

### LXI.

### LXIV.

BUT the **Empirical** type of philosophy produces dogmas <note>original: *placita*; the settled opinions or doctrines of a school.</note> more deformed and monstrous than the **Sophistical** or rational type. This is because it is not based in the light of common notions (which, although thin and superficial, are nonetheless somewhat universal and pertain to many things), but is instead founded in the narrowness and obscurity of a few experiments. Therefore, such a philosophy seems probable and almost certain to those who are daily engaged in such experiments and have infected their imagination with them; to everyone else, it seems incredible and vain.

A notable example of this is found in the **Chemists** <note>original: *Chymicis*; here referring to the alchemists of the early 17th century.</note> and their doctrines; otherwise, it is hardly found at this time, except perhaps in the philosophy of **Gilbert** <note>William Gilbert (1544–1603), an English scientist. *   If a body, otherwise unchanged, is moved in place, this is *Local Motion*.
*   If its place and species remain the same, but it is changed in quality, this is *Alteration*.
*   If, however, by that change the mass itself and the quantity of the body do not remain the same, this is the motion of *Growth* and *Diminution*.
*   If they are changed so significantly that they change their very species and substance and pass into another, this is *Generation* and *Corruption*.

But these are merely popular notions and in no way penetrate into Nature; they are only measures and periods of time, not actual species of motion. For they suggest "how far" a thing has gone, but not "in what manner" or "from what source" it moves. For neither...

In the sciences, throughout so many centuries, it is difficult to point to a single experiment intended to relieve and improve the human condition that can be truly credited to the speculations and doctrines of philosophy.

*Celsus* <note>Aulus Cornelius Celsus (c. 25 BC – c. 50 AD) was a Roman medical encyclopedist whose work was highly regarded during the Renaissance for its clarity and practical focus.</note> candidly and wisely admits this: namely, that the practical applications of medicine were discovered first, and only afterward did men philosophize about them, searching for and assigning causes. It did not happen in the reverse order—that philosophy and the knowledge of causes led to the discovery of the experiments themselves.

Therefore, it was not surprising that among the Egyptians (who granted divinity and sacred status to the inventors of things) there were more images of wild animals than of men. This is because animals, through their natural instincts, have produced many discoveries, whereas men, through their discourses and rational conclusions, have provided few or none.

The diligence of the <term>chemists</term> <note>original: *Chymicorum*. In Bacon's time, this referred to alchemists, who sought to transform matter through trial and error.</note> has produced some results; however, these occurred as if by chance and in passing, or through a certain variation of trials (as craftsmen often do), rather than from any formal art or theory. For the theories they have invented actually disturb and confuse experiments rather than assisting them. Among those who deal in what they call <term>Natural Magic</term> <note>A branch of study aimed at using the "hidden" powers of nature, often criticized by Bacon for lacking a rigorous, reproducible method.</note>, few inventions are found; and those are trivial and closer to fraud. Therefore, just as it is cautioned in Religion that Faith [must be] shown by Works <note>A reference to the biblical Epistle of James: "Faith without works is dead." ### LXXIV.
Signs should also be drawn from the growth and progress of philosophies and sciences. For things founded upon Nature grow and increase; however, things founded upon mere Opinion change, but do not grow. Therefore, if these doctrines had not been like plants torn away from their roots, but instead remained attached to the womb of Nature and were nourished by her, then that which we have seen occurring for two thousand years now would never have happened: namely, that the sciences remain stuck in their own tracks and stay in nearly the same state, having achieved no noteworthy growth. On the contrary, they flourished most under their first author <note>Original: "in primo Authore"; Bacon is likely referring to ancient Greek philosophers like Aristotle, whose followers he believed had merely repeated his work rather than expanding upon it.</note> and subsequently declined. In the **Mechanical Arts** <term>Mechanical Arts: Practical crafts, engineering, and technologies, such as printing, gunpowder, or the compass.</term>, however, which are founded upon Nature and the light of **Experience**, we see the opposite occur. These arts (as long as they are favored) are filled, as it were, with a certain vital spirit, and they continually thrive and grow; at first they are crude, then convenient, later refined, and perpetually improved.
