LXXV.
Another **Sign** must also be considered; (if indeed the name "Sign" is suitable for this, since it is rather a **Testimony**, and indeed the most powerful of all testimonies); this is the personal confession of the very authors whom people follow today. For even those who pronounce judgment on matters with such great confidence, nevertheless, at intervals—when they return to their senses—turn to making complaints about the subtlety of Nature, the obscurity of things, and the weakness of the human intellect. If this were done with simple honesty, it might perhaps deter those who are more timid from further inquiry; yet it might sharpen and incite others, who possess a more spirited and confident nature, toward further progress. 

However, it is not enough for these authors to confess their own limitations. Instead, whatever has remained unknown or untouched by themselves or their masters, they place beyond the boundaries of what is **Possible**. They pronounce such things impossible to know or to do—as if speaking with the authority of their "art." With the greatest pride and envy, they turn the weakness of their own discoveries into a slander against Nature herself, leading everyone else into despair. From this attitude arose the school of the New Academy, which openly held to **Incomprehensibility** <note>original: "Acatalepsiam"; the philosophical doctrine that nothing can be known with absolute certainty</note> and condemned humanity to eternal darkness. From this also comes the opinion that **Forms**—or the true differences between things (which are in truth the laws of <term>pure act</term> <note>Bacon refers here to the fundamental, underlying laws or patterns of motion and nature that define what a thing is and what it does</note>)—are impossible to discover and are beyond the reach of man.

From this arise those opinions in the **Active and Operative** <term>Active and Operative: The practical side of science focused on producing results and transforming nature, rather than just passive observation.</term> part of science: that the Heat of the Sun and the Heat of Fire differ fundamentally in kind. This is claimed so that humans do not think they can produce or shape anything similar to the works of Nature through the use of Fire. From this also comes the saying: that **Composition** <note>The simple putting together of parts.</note> is only the work of Man, but **True Mixing** <note>original: *Mistionem*; refers to a deeper, chemical-like union of substances.</note> is the work of Nature alone. This is said so that men do not hope for any generation or transformation of natural bodies through human art. Therefore, by this sign, men will easily be persuaded not to entangle their fortunes and hard work with dogmas that are not only hopeless, but actually dedicated to despair.

### LXXVI.

Nor should this **Sign** <note>Bacon uses "signs" like a doctor looks for symptoms; these are the indicators that the current way of doing science is "sick."</note> be overlooked: that there was once such great disagreement among philosophers and such a variety of different Schools. This shows clearly enough that the path from the **Senses** to the **Intellect** was not well-paved, since the same subject matter of philosophy (namely, the nature of things) was pulled apart into such wandering and multiple errors. And although in these current times, disagreements and diversities of dogmas regarding the fundamental Principles and entire systems of philosophy have mostly died out, nevertheless, regarding the specific parts of philosophy, countless questions and controversies remain. Thus it is plain to see that there is nothing certain or sound, neither in the philosophies themselves nor in the methods used for **Demonstration** <term>Demonstration: The logical process or proof used to show that a conclusion follows from its premises.</term>.

# APHORISMS
concerning the
# PREPARATION OF A PRIMARY HISTORY

## APHORISM I.

**N**ature is placed in a threefold state and undergoes a triple governance. Either she is free, and unfolds herself in her ordinary course; or she is driven from her natural state by the depravities and insolences of matter, and by the violence of obstacles; or she is constrained and molded by art <note>original: "arte"; in this context, "art" refers to human skill, technology, and craft</note> and human service.

And that first state refers to the *Species of things*; the second to *Monsters* <note>original: "Monstra"; Bacon uses this term to describe biological rarities or deviations from the natural norm, what we might call "freaks of nature" today</note>; the third to *Artificial things*. For in artificial things, Nature accepts a yoke from the command of Man: for those things would never have been made without Man. But through the labor and service of Man, an entirely new face of bodies is seen, and as it were another universe of things, or another theater. 

Thus, Natural History is threefold. For it treats either the *Freedom* of Nature, or her *Errors*, or her *Bonds*; so that we may correctly divide it into the History of *Generations*, *Preter-generations* <term>Preter-generations: literally "beyond generations," referring to anomalies, mutations, and natural wonders that deviate from the standard laws of reproduction and growth</term>, and *Arts*; the last of which we have also become accustomed to call *Mechanical* and *Experimental*. 

Nor yet that

...we instruct that these three <note>Bacon refers here to the "Generations" (nature's normal course), "Pretergenerations" (nature's errors or monsters), and "Arts" (nature altered by man).</note> should be treated separately. For why should the **Histories of Monsters** not be joined with the **History of the Species** themselves in each instance? Even **Artificial things** <note>original: "Artificialia"; referring to man-made artifacts or experimental results.</note> are sometimes rightly joined with the Species, and sometimes better separated. Therefore, it is best to take counsel on these matters as they arise from the subject itself. For strict methodology produces repetitions and wordiness, equally where there is too much of it as where there is none.

### II.

**Natural History**, as it is threefold in its Subject (as we have said), so it is **twofold in its Use**. For it is employed either for the **Knowledge of things themselves**, which are entrusted to History; or as the primary **Material of Philosophy**, and the furniture or "forest" <note>original: "Sylva"; Bacon frequently uses this term to describe a collection of raw data or a "storehouse" of facts.</note> of **true Induction** <term>Induction: The logical process of reaching a general conclusion by observing specific examples, a cornerstone of the "Baconian" scientific method.</term>.

And it is this latter purpose that is now being addressed; **Now**, I say; and never before this. For neither *Aristotle*, nor *Theophrastus*, nor *Dioscorides*, nor *Pliny the Elder*, and much less the *moderns*, ever proposed this end (of which we speak) for Natural History. And it is of the utmost importance that those who hereafter take upon themselves the task of writing Natural History should constantly think on this, and turn it over in their minds: that they ought not to serve the **reader's pleasure**, nor even the **utility** which might be gained from the Narrations at present, but should seek out and bring together a **Wealth** and variety...

<summary>Francis Bacon argues that Natural History should serve as the raw data for scientific induction rather than just for entertainment or immediate practical use, distinguishing his method from ancient naturalists.</summary>

### III.

Since this undertaking is a matter of great effort and labor, it is only right that it should not be weighed down with unnecessary things. There are, therefore, three things about which people must be clearly warned, so that they might apply their efforts to them only very sparingly; for these are things that increase the sheer mass of the work immensely, but do little or nothing to advance its effectiveness.

First, then, let us dispense with antiquities <note>meaning ancient historical accounts or myths</note>, and citations, or the testimonies of authors; also disputes, controversies, and differing opinions; in short, all things philological <term>Philological: here referring to the scholarly study of books and traditional learning rather than the direct study of nature</term>. For an author should not be cited unless the matter is of doubtful reliability; nor should a controversy be introduced, except in a matter of great importance. As for those things that concern the ornaments of speech, similes, the "treasures of eloquence," and such vanities, let them be rejected entirely. Furthermore, everything that is included should be set forth briefly and concisely, so that they are nothing but the facts themselves <note>original: "nihil minus sint quam verba", literally "nothing less than words," suggesting a density of meaning where no word is wasted and only the essential information remains</note>. For no one who collects and stores materials for buildings, ships, or other such structures arranges and displays them beautifully (as one does in a shop) to please the onlooker; instead, he is only concerned that they be sound and good,

### IV.

In the **History** which we require and intend in our mind, we must see above all else that it is widely inclusive, and made to the **Measure of the Universe**. For the World must not be narrowed to the cramped limits of the Intellect (as has been done until now), but the Intellect must be expanded and opened up to receive the **Image of the World** exactly as it is found. For we altogether relegate the superstitious *History of Miracles* (of whatever kind it may be) to its own treatise; nor should it be undertaken right from the start, but a little later when we have penetrated deeper into the Investigation of Nature.

But as for the *History of Arts*, and of Nature altered and changed by Man, or *Experimental History*, we establish it as threefold. For it is either drawn from the Mechanical Arts; or from the operative part of the Liberal Sciences; or from various practices and experiments which have not yet formed into a proper Art; indeed, which sometimes arise from the most common experience, nor...

### V.

Among those parts of History which we have mentioned, the **History of Arts** is of the greatest use, because it exhibits things in motion and leads more directly to <term>Praxis</term> <note>Practical application or "doing."</note>. Furthermore, it pulls away the mask and the veil from natural objects, which are usually hidden or obscured under a variety of shapes and external appearances. Finally, the "vexations" <note>The ways humans manipulate or "disturb" nature through experimentation.</note> of Art are certainly like the chains and manacles of ***Proteus***, <note>In Greek mythology, Proteus was a shape-shifting sea god; he would only tell the truth if he was bound and held fast through all his transformations.</note> which betray the ultimate struggles and efforts of matter. For physical bodies do not wish to be destroyed or annihilated; rather, they change themselves into various forms. Therefore, regarding this History—even though it may appear **Mechanical** and less "liberal" <note>Bacon is challenging the prejudice of his time, which viewed manual crafts as inferior to the "liberal arts" studied by gentlemen.</note>—the greatest diligence must be applied, setting aside all arrogance and pride.

Again, among the Arts, those are to be preferred which display, alter, and prepare natural bodies and the materials of things; such as **Agriculture**; **Cookery**; **Chemistry**; **Dyeing**; Workmanship— <note>The Latin text cuts off at "Opi-", likely "Opificia" or "Opificum" (workmanship/crafts).</note>

<summary>Bacon argues that a complete natural history must include human crafts and technology, as manipulating nature ("vexing" it) reveals its true properties better than simple observation. He urges scholars to overcome their intellectual snobbery against "mechanical" labor.</summary>

Truly, in the entire collection of this *History of the Arts*, this point must be entirely cautioned and thoroughly committed to memory: that the Experiments of the Arts are to be received not only as they lead to the specific goal of the Art, but also as they intervene in any other way. For example, the fact that Lobsters <note>original: "Locustae" — in this context, this refers to sea-lobsters rather than grasshoppers.</note> or Crabs, which previously resembled the color of mud, turn red when cooked, is of no importance to the dinner table; yet this very instance is nonetheless useful for investigating the nature of Redness, since the same thing also happens in fired Bricks. Similarly, the fact that Meats are salted with less delay in winter than in summer is not only significant for the Cook to season food well and sufficiently, but is also a good instance for indicating the nature and impression of Cold. For this reason, anyone who thinks that our intention is satisfied by merely looking at the end results of an art will have wandered, as the saying goes, as far as the heavens <note>original: "toto caelo erraverit" — a Latin idiom meaning to be completely and utterly mistaken.</note>.

### VI.

**R**epeat must also be made here of what we treated more extensively in *Aphorisms* 99, 119, and 120 of the *First Book*; here, however, in the manner of a rule, it should suffice to command briefly. That is: there should be received into this History, first, the most common things, which one might think redundant to include in writing because they are so familiarly known. Next, things that are low, illiberal, or even foul; (<note>original: "Omnia enim munda mundis"</note> *for to the pure, all things are pure*; and if profit from urine <note>A reference to the Roman Emperor Vespasian, who famously argued that "money does not smell" even when derived from a tax on public latrines.</note> has a good odor, how much more so do light and information gained from any subject whatever?). Also include things that are light and childish; (and no wonder, for we must plainly <note>original: "repueraſcendum"</note> become like children again). Finally, include things that seem to be of an excessive subtlety, appearing to have no use in themselves. For the things proposed in this History (as has already been said) are not gathered for their own sake; therefore, it is not right to measure their value based on the things themselves.

### VII.

Furthermore, we command that all things in Nature—both Bodies and **Virtues** <note>Bacon uses "virtues" to refer to the active powers, properties, or forces of objects</note>—should be set forth (as far as possible) numbered, weighed, measured, and defined. For we are contemplating **Works** <note>Meaning practical applications, inventions, or results</note>, not Speculations. Now, Physics and Mathematics, when well combined, generate **Practice** <note>Applied science or technology</note>. Therefore, the exact **revolutions** <note>original: "Restitutiones," referring to the time it takes for a planet to return to a specific point in its orbit</note> and distances of the Planets should be recorded in the *History of Heavenly Bodies*; the circumference of the Earth, and how much of the surface it occupies in respect to the Waters, in the *History of Earth and Sea*; how much compression the Air can suffer without strong <term>resistance</term> <note>original: "Antitypia," a Greek-derived term for the quality of matter that resists being penetrated or compressed</note>, in the *History of Air*; how much one metal outweighs another, in the *History of Metals*; and innumerable things of that kind must be sought out and written down. 

When, however, exact proportions cannot be obtained, then we must certainly resort to estimates or indefinite comparisons. For instance (if perhaps we distrust the calculations of Astronomers regarding distances), we might state that the Moon is below the shadow of the Earth; that Mercury is above...

VIII.

**R**egarding the reliability of those things which are to be received into the History: it is necessary that they be of either **certain** reliability, **doubtful** reliability, or **condemned** reliability. The first type should be set down simply. The second type with a note; namely, by the phrase *It is related*, or *They report*, or *I have heard from a trustworthy source*, and the like. For it would be too laborious to write down the arguments for reliability on either side, and it will undoubtedly delay the writer too much. Nor does it matter much for the work at hand: because (as we said in *Aphorism 118, Book 1*) the truth of the **axioms** <note>general principles or laws of nature derived from observation</note> will shortly afterward refute the falsehood of experiments, unless those falsehoods are everywhere abundant. Nevertheless, if an **instance** <term>Instance: a specific example or case study used to illustrate or prove a natural law</term> should be more noble, either for its practical use or because many other things might depend upon it, then the **author** must certainly be named; and not merely nakedly, but with some mention of whether they wrote from **report**, or...

->**IX.**<-

There remain certain additions useful for **Natural History**, which may more conveniently guide and adapt it to the work of the <term>Interpreter</term><note>Bacon refers to the "Interpreter of Nature," the person who uses these collected facts to discover the underlying laws of the universe.</note>, which follows. These are five in number.

**First**, **Questions** (I do not mean of Causes, but of Fact) should be added, to provoke and solicit further inquiry. For example, in a **History of the Earth and Sea**: whether the Caspian Sea ebbs and flows, and at what hourly interval; whether there is any **Southern Continent**<note>original: "Continens Australis." In the 17th century, the existence of a massive southern landmass was still a subject of geographical debate.</note>, or rather an island; and similar matters.

**Second**, in any new and more subtle **Experiment**, the very method of the experiment which was used should be added. This is so that men’s judgment may be free to decide whether the information gathered from that experiment is reliable or deceptive, and also that men’s industry may be stimulated to seek out more accurate methods, if possible.

**Third**, if there is any doubt or hesitation in a narrative, we do not want it suppressed or kept silent at all, but plainly and clearly noted, in the place of a **Note** or **Warning**. For we desire that the primary history be written most religiously, as if an oath had been taken regarding its truth in every detail—since it is the **Volume of the Works of God** and (as much as the Majesty of Divine things...

### X.

AND these shall suffice as far as general Precepts are concerned: which, if they are diligently observed, this Work of History will both head straight for its goal and not grow beyond measure. 404      Catalog of Particular Histories

**I**t is worth noting that since many experiments will necessarily fall under two or more headings (for example, the History of Plants and the History of the Art of Gardening <note>original: "Historia Plantarum, & Historia Artis Hortulanæ"</note> will share much in common), it is more convenient to conduct the investigation through the Arts <note>In this context, "Arts" refers to human crafts, technologies, and methods of manipulating nature.</note>, while the final arrangement should be organized by Bodies <note>Bacon refers to "Bodies" as the physical subjects or substances of the natural world, rather than human activities.</note>. We care little for the mechanical arts in and of themselves; we value them only for what they contribute to the building of Philosophy <note>To Bacon, "Philosophy" meant natural science—the systematic study and understanding of the physical world.</note>. However, these matters will be better managed as the project unfolds.

### Aphorism XIII.

Third, a presentation must be made to the Intellect of **Instances** <note>Bacon uses "Instances" as specific examples or data points for scientific observation.</note> in which the **Nature** under investigation is present to a greater or lesser degree; whether the comparison is made by observing increase and decrease within the same subject, or by comparing different subjects with one another. For since the **Form** <term>Form: In Bacon’s thought, the "Form" is the underlying physical law or essence that produces a specific quality like heat.</term> of a thing is the **thing itself** <note>original: *ipsissima Res*</note>; and the Thing does not differ from the Form except as the *Apparent* differs from the *Existent*, or the *Outer* from the *Inner*, or in relation to *Man* versus in relation to the *Universe*; it follows absolutely that no nature should be accepted as a true Form unless it always decreases when the nature itself decreases, and likewise always increases when the nature itself increases. Therefore, we have become accustomed to calling this table the **Table of Degrees**, or the **Table of Comparison**.

->**Table of Degrees, or Comparison regarding Heat.**<-

### NEW ORGANON. 179

...and preparation for heat. Later, we shall finally descend to those things which are actually hot, or hot to the touch, and their intensities and degrees.

1. In solid and tangible bodies, nothing is found which is originally hot in its own nature. <note>Bacon is arguing that inanimate matter does not possess heat as an inherent property; it must be acting or being acted upon to become warm.</note> For no stone, no metal, no sulfur, no <term>mineral</term> <note>original: "fossile"; in the 17th century, this referred to any substance dug from the earth, including minerals and ores, rather than just prehistoric remains.</note>, no wood, no water, and no animal corpse is found to be hot. As for the hot waters in <term>baths</term> <note>original: "Balneis"; referring here to natural thermal springs.</note>, they appear to be heated by accident, either by flame or subterranean fire—such as that vomited from Etna and several other mountains—or from the <term>clash of substances</term> <note>original: "conflictu corporum"; Bacon is referring to exothermic chemical reactions, such as those caused by acids dissolving metals.</note>, just as heat is produced during the dissolution of iron and tin. Therefore, the degree of heat in inanimate objects, as perceived by human touch, is zero; nevertheless, these objects differ in their degree of cold; for wood is not as cold as metal. But this belongs to the *Table of Degrees of Cold*.

2. However, regarding potential heats and readiness for flame, many inanimate things are found to be quite predisposed, such as sulfur, <term>naphtha</term> <note>A volatile, flammable liquid hydrocarbon.</note>, and petroleum.

3. Things that were previously heated, such as horse manure from an animal, or lime, or perhaps ash or soot from a fire, retain certain latent remains of their former heat. <note>Horse manure was frequently used by early chemists and alchemists as a source of gentle, steady heat for "digesting" substances.</note> Therefore, certain distillations and separations of bo- <insert>dies</insert> <note>The text cuts off here at the signature mark "H 6", preparing for the word "corporum" on the next page.</note>

### XV.

And the work and duty of these three tables we are accustomed to call the *Presentation of Instances to the Intellect*. Once the *Presentation* is made, <term>Induction</term> <note>The process of reaching a general conclusion from specific observations.</note> itself must be set to work. For we must find, based on the *Presentation* of each and every instance, a certain Nature <note>By "Nature," Bacon means a fundamental quality or property of a thing.</note> that is always present, absent, or increases and decreases along with the nature under investigation; and which is (as said before) a limitation of a more common nature.

If the mind attempts to do this affirmatively from the start (which it always tends to do when left to its own devices), there will arise phantoms, mere opinions, poorly defined notions, and <term>Axioms</term> <note>Established principles or self-evident truths.</note> that require daily correction; unless one prefers (after the fashion of the <term>Schools</term>) <note>original: "Scholarum more"; referring to the traditional Scholastic philosophers of the Middle Ages who relied on logic and dogma rather than physical evidence.</note> to fight for what is false. These results will undoubtedly be better or worse depending on the capability and strength of the intellect doing the work. 

But it belongs only to God (the Giver and Maker of <term>Forms</term>) <note>In Bacon's philosophy, a "Form" is the internal law or essential nature that governs a physical property like heat or light.</note>, or perhaps to Angels and higher Intelligences, to know Forms immediately through affirmation, right from the start of contemplation. But it is certainly beyond the power of man; to whom it is only granted to proceed first by *Negatives*, and only in the last place to arrive at *Affirmatives*, after every possible kind of exclusion has been made.

### XVI. 

Thus...

<summary>Bacon explains that while God may perceive the essence of things immediately, humans must use "Induction" by first ruling out what is false (the negative) before they can arrive at the truth (the affirmative).</summary>

XVI.
Therefore, a complete dismantling and separation of Nature must be performed; certainly not by Fire <note>original: "per Ignem". Bacon is contrasting the "fire" used by alchemists in their furnaces with the intellectual "fire" of the human mind.</note>, but by the Mind, as if by a divine Fire. Thus, the first task of <term>true Induction|A method of reasoning that moves from specific observations to general truths by systematically testing and eliminating false hypotheses</term> (so far as discovering <term>Forms|The fundamental laws or internal structures that produce a specific quality, such as heat or light</term> is concerned) is the *Rejection or Exclusion* of individual natures which are not found in some Instance where the given nature is present. Or they are found in some Instance where the given nature is absent; or they are found to increase in some Instance when the given nature decreases; or decrease when the given nature increases. Then indeed, after the *Rejection and Exclusion* have been performed in the proper ways, there will remain in the second place (as if at the bottom, while volatile opinions vanish like smoke) a Form that is affirmative, solid, true, and well-defined. This is easy to say, but it is reached through many winding paths. We, however, shall perhaps omit nothing of those things which contribute to this.

   For first, regarding compound Forms <note>original: "Formis copulatis". These are the complex structures of whole objects, like a lion or gold, rather than single qualities.</note>, which are (as we said) made of simple Natures <note>Simple natures are basic qualities like heat, weight, color, or density.</note>

We are not speaking at present of those unions that arise from the common course of the universe—such as the nature of the Lion, the Eagle, the Rose, Gold, and the like <note>original: "Leonis, Aquilæ, Rosæ, Auri." For when we speak of Forms, we mean nothing other than those laws and determinations of pure activity <term>actus purus: the actual manifestation or operation of a thing's nature in the physical world</term> which organize and constitute any simple nature; such as heat, light, or weight, in every kind of matter and subject capable of receiving them. Therefore, the Form of Heat or the Form of Light is the same thing as the Law of Heat or the Law of Light. Indeed, we never withdraw or abstract our focus from the things themselves and the practical, operative side of science. ...pushed back, repelled, and reverberated; so that it takes on an alternating motion, perpetually trembling, struggling, and striving, and irritated by the repercussion; from which that fury of Fire and Heat has its origin.

This *Difference* <note>original: "Differentia" — in logic, this refers to the specific characteristic that distinguishes a species from others in the same category.</note> is shown especially in Flame and boiling Liquids: which perpetually tremble, swell in small portions, and then subside again.

It is also shown in those bodies which are of such hard structure that, when heated or Ignited, they do not swell or expand in mass; such as red-hot Iron, in which Heat is most intense.

It is also shown in this: that during the coldest weather, a hearth fire burns most fiercely. <note>Bacon refers to the contemporary observation that fires seem more vigorous in winter, which he attributes to the surrounding cold "confining" the heat and increasing its internal struggle.</note>

It is also shown in this: that when Air is expanded in a weather-glass <note>original: "vitrum Calendari" — a thermoscope, an early ancestor of the thermometer that measured the expansion of air.</note> without hindrance or repulsion—namely, uniformly and equally—no Heat is perceived. Even in trapped winds, although they burst out with the greatest force, no significant Heat is perceived; because the Motion happens as a whole, without that alternating Motion among the particles. And to this end, let an Experiment be made to see whether Flame does not burn more sharply toward the sides than in the middle of the flame.

It is also shown in this, that all burning is carried out through the minute pores of the body.

### XXIII.

Among the prerogative Instances, we will place in the second rank *Migratory Instances*. These are instances in which the nature being investigated <term>Natura Inquisita|The specific physical quality or property, such as heat or whiteness, that the scientist is currently trying to define</term> migrates toward generation <note>coming into existence</note> when it did not previously exist; or, conversely, migrates toward corruption <note>fading away or ceasing to be</note> when it previously existed. A *Clandestine Instance* <note>Bacon defines these as instances where a nature or quality is exhibited in its weakest and most hidden form</note> however is a magnet "armed" with iron <note>original: "magnes ferro armatus"; this refers to the practice of capping a lodestone with iron plates to concentrate and increase its lifting power</note>, or rather the iron within an armed magnet. This occurs because of the similarity of the substance of wood to wood, even though this [capacity] previously lay hidden in the wood. Likewise, although air does not visibly attract air, nor water attract water in large, whole bodies; nevertheless, a bubble brought close to another bubble dissolves that bubble more easily than if the other were absent, because of the appetite for <term>Coition</term> of water with water, and air with air. And *Clandestine Instances* of this kind (which are of the most noble use, as has been said) reveal themselves most clearly in small and subtle portions of bodies.

### XXVI.

Among the <term>Prerogative Instances</term> <note>These are "privileged" examples or observations that carry more weight than others in scientific induction.</note>, we shall place in the fifth position ***Constitutive Instances***, which we are also accustomed to call ***Manipular Instances*** <note>Latin: *Manipulares*. These are instances that constitute a single species of the nature being investigated, acting as a "minor form." 

Since legitimate Forms (which are always interchangeable with the natures under investigation) lie hidden deep within and are not easily discovered, the reality of the situation and the weakness of the human intellect require that we do not neglect "particular forms." These particular forms group together certain *bundles* <note>original: "Manipulorum"</note> of instances (though certainly not all of them) into a common notion. Therefore, instances that are useful for this purpose possess no small power and hold a certain prerogative.

Finally, this must be absolutely commanded and frequently reminded: that human diligence in the **Investigation and Gathering of <term>Natural History</term>** <note>The systematic study of animals, plants, and minerals</note> should from now on be completely changed, and turned into the opposite of what is currently in use. ### XXXII.

From what has been said before, it is clear that those five classes of instances of which we have spoken (<note>original: "vid. Instantiarum Conformium, Instantiarum Monadicarum, Instantiarum Deviantium, Instantiarum Limitanearum, Instantiarum Potestatis"</note> *see: Conformable Instances, Monadic Instances, Deviating Instances, Bordering Instances, and Instances of Power*) ought not to be reserved until a specific Nature <note>In Bacon’s work, a "Nature" refers to a physical property or quality being studied, such as heat, weight, or color.</note> is investigated. The remaining instances which we proposed in the first place—and many of those which follow—must be set aside for specific inquiries; however, these five should be collected immediately from the very start.

They should be gathered as a kind of particular *History*. This is because they organize the information that enters the Intellect and correct the warped disposition of the Intellect itself. Without this correction, the mind is inevitably saturated, infected, and finally perverted and distorted by the daily and customary impressions it encounters.

Therefore, these instances should be applied as a sort of preparation to rectify and cleanse the Intellect. For whatever draws the Intellect away from its usual habits levels and smooths its surface <note>original: "aream ejus" — Bacon uses the metaphor of a field or "area" that must be cleared and leveled before true work can begin.</note> so that it may receive the Dry Light <note>original: "Lumen siccum" — a concept from Heraclitus that Bacon used to describe intellect unclouded by the "moisture" of passions or personal biases.</note> and pure light of true notions.

Moreover, instances of this kind pave and prepare the way for the Operational <note>original: "Operativam" — the active, practical side of science that produces results.</note> part of science, as we shall explain in its proper place when we discuss the *Deductions to Practice*.

->XXXIII.<-

Among the *Prerogatives of Instances*, we place in the eleventh position *Instances of Companionship* and of *Enmity*; which we have also been accustomed to call *Instances of Fixed Propositions*. These are instances which exhibit some Body or concrete thing in which the Nature Under Investigation <note>original: "Natura Inquisita" — the specific quality or "form" Bacon is trying to define, such as heat, light, or weight.</note> perpetually follows as an inseparable companion. Or, on the contrary, they show a body in which the Nature Under Investigation perpetually flees and is excluded from its *Companionship*, as an *Enemy* and foe.

For from instances of this kind, certain and universal propositions are formed, whether *Affirmative* or *Negative*: in which the Subject will be such a concrete body, and the Predicate will be the Nature Under Investigation itself. For particular propositions are not at all "fixed" where the Nature Under Investigation is found in some concrete thing to be fleeting and mobile—namely, as something arriving or Acquired <note>original: "Accedens, sive Acquisita"</note>; or again, as something retreating or Abandoned <note>original: "Recedens, sive Deposita"</note>. 

Therefore, particular propositions do not hold any great *Prerogative* <note>A "prerogative" here refers to a special privilege or higher importance in providing evidence for a scientific conclusion.</note>, except only in the *Case of Migration* <note>original: "Casu Migrationis" — Bacon's 8th type of instance, where a nature is observed while it is in the process of appearing or disappearing, like the color of water when it turns into foam.</note>; which was discussed earlier. And nevertheless, even those particular propositions, when compared and collated with Universal ones, are very helpful, as will be discussed in its proper place. However, even in these Universal Propositions, we do not require an exact or absolute Affirmation or Negation.

The use of *Instances of Companionship* <note>original: "Instantiarum Comitatus"; these are examples where a specific quality is always present alongside the nature being studied, acting as a constant companion.</note> is to narrow down the *Affirmative of the Form* <term>Form: in Bacon’s philosophy, the "Form" is the fundamental law or internal structure that causes a specific quality (like heat or light) to exist.</term>.

For we have no sensory knowledge of the depths of the Earth; but of those bodies which are known to us, there is no composition at all that is not capable of receiving Heat.

...stance: the *Hostile Instance* <note>original: *Instantia Hostilis*</note> is Air. For metal can flow and can stay firm; similarly glass; even water can stay firm when it freezes: but it is impossible for Air ever to stay firm or cast off its fluidity.

But regarding *Instances* of these types of *fixed propositions*, two warnings remain that are useful for the task at hand. First, if a completely universal *Affirmative* or *Negative* is missing, that very fact should be diligently noted as a Non-Entity <note>original: *Non-Ens*; something that does not exist in the natural order known to us</note>: just as we did regarding Heat, where a *Universal Negative* (at least regarding the entities that have come to our knowledge) is missing in the nature of things. <note>Bacon observes that we do not know of any physical object that is completely and fundamentally devoid of all heat.</note> Similarly, if the Nature being investigated is "Eternal" or "Incorruptible," a Universal Affirmative is missing here among us. For neither *Eternal* nor *Incorruptible* can be predicated <note>term: predicated — asserted as a property or characteristic of a subject</note> of any of those bodies which are below the Heavens or above the interior of the Earth. 

The second Warning is that to Universal Propositions—both Affirmative and Negative—regarding any Concrete thing, those Concrete things should be added which seem to come closest to that which is among the Non-Entities: as in *Heat*, the softest flames and those that burn the least; in the *Incorruptible*, *Gold*, which comes closest to that state. For all these things indicate the boundaries of Nature between Being and Non-Being; and they help in the Circumscriptions <note>term: Circumscription — the act of defining the limits or boundaries of a concept or "Form"</note> of Forms, so that they do not slip away and wander outside the conditions of Matter.

### XXXIV.
Among the **Prerogative Instances**, we will place in the twelfth position those very **Subjunctive Instances** <term>Subjunctive Instances: Cases that are "subjoined" or attached to general rules to show their exceptions or boundaries</term>, which we discussed in a previous Aphorism: we have also become accustomed to calling them **Instances of Ultimacy** or **of the Limit**. For these types of instances are not only useful when they are subjoined to fixed propositions, but also in their own right and by their own nature. For they indicate quite clearly the true divisions of Nature and the measures of things, showing exactly "how far" Nature acts or endures, and thereafter the transitions of Nature into something else. Such examples include: **Gold**, in weight; **Iron**, in hardness; the **Whale**, in the size of animals; the **Dog**, in the sense of smell; the **Combustion of Gunpowder**, in rapid expansion; and others of that kind. Nor should those things which represent the lowest degree of the scale be displayed any less than those of the highest: such as **Spirit of Wine** <note>original: "Spiritus vini," referring to high-proof distilled alcohol</note>, in weight; **Silk**, in softness; the **Skin-mites** <note>original: "Vermiculi cutis," likely referring to microscopic mites or small parasites</note>, in the size of animals; and the rest.

### XXXV.
Among the **Prerogative Instances**, we will place in the thirteenth position **Instances of Alliance** or **of Union**. These are those which blend and unite "Natures" <note>Bacon uses the word "Natures" to mean fundamental physical properties or qualities</note> that are commonly thought to be heterogeneous <note>original: "Heterogeneæ," meaning entirely different in kind or origin</note>, and are marked and designated as such by the accepted divisions of the day.

<summary>Bacon defines the 12th and 13th types of "Prerogative Instances," focusing on the extremes of nature (the greatest and smallest examples of a quality) and instances that bridge seemingly unrelated categories.</summary>

--- Page 199 ---
<meta>This page continues Bacon’s classification of "Prerogative Instances"—specific types of observations or experiments that hold special power in guiding the intellect toward true scientific understanding. This section introduces the Instances of Alliance.</meta>

->NEW ORGANON. 247<-

But *Instances of Alliance* <note>original: "Instantiæ Fœderis"; these are examples that reveal connections between things previously thought to be completely different</note> show that operations and effects which are usually attributed to one of those heterogeneous <term>heterogeneous: things that are fundamentally different in kind or nature</term> categories as being unique to it, also belong to others among those categories. This is to prove that this supposed heterogeneity (which is the common opinion) is not real or essential, but is nothing other than a modification of a common nature. These instances are therefore most useful for lifting and raising the intellect from specific differences to general kinds, and for removing the masks and phantoms of things as they appear and present themselves disguised in concrete substances.

For example: let the nature under investigation be Heat. There appears to be a standard and authoritative division into three kinds of heat: namely, the Heat of Celestial bodies <note>the sun and stars</note>, the Heat of Animals, and the Heat of Fire. It is believed that these heats (especially one of them compared to the other two) are different in their very essence and kind—or specific nature—and are plainly heterogeneous. This is because celestial and animal heat generate and nourish life, whereas the heat of fire, on the contrary, corrupts and destroys.

An *Instance of Alliance* is therefore that well-known experiment where a branch of a vine is brought inside a house where there is a constant fire, from which the grapes ripen even a whole month earlier than those outside. Thus, the ripening of fruit, even while still hanging on the tree, can be achieved by fire, even though this very task seems to be the unique work of the Sun.

Similarly, let the **Nature under Investigation** be **Weight**. 

There is a commonly accepted division: that Dense and Solid bodies are carried toward the center of the Earth, while Rare and Thin bodies are carried toward the circumference of the Heavens, as if to their own "proper places." And as for these "places"—though such ideas are accepted in the Schools <note>The "Schools" refers to the traditional universities of the time which taught Aristotelian philosophy.</note>—it is a clearly foolish and childish thought that a "Place" can have any power. Therefore, philosophers talk nonsense when they say that if the Earth were bored through, heavy bodies would stop moving once they reached the Center. For that Center would certainly be a powerful and effective kind of *Nothing*, or a mathematical point, which could either act upon other things or be desired by them in turn; but a body is not acted upon except by another body. 

In truth, this desire for **Ascending** and **Descending** is found either in the configuration <term>Schematism: the internal structure or arrangement of a substance</term> of the body that moves, or in a sympathy or agreement with another body. It is necessary that when there is a High Tide <term>Fluxus; the flow or rising of the tide</term> in one part of the sea, there occurs at the same time a Low Tide <term>Refluxus; the ebb or receding of the tide</term> somewhere else in the sea. Therefore, the inquiry is reduced to this point. But *Acosta* <note>José de Acosta (1540–1600) was a Spanish Jesuit naturalist whose observations in the New World were highly influential for early modern scientists like Bacon.</note> observed, along with several others (after a diligent inquiry was made), that on the shores of Florida and on the opposite shores of Spain and Africa, the High Tides occur at the same times, and the Low Tides likewise occur at the same times. It is not the opposite—where a high tide on the coast of Florida would result in a low tide on the coasts of Spain and Africa.

However, to one paying even closer attention, this does not necessarily prove a Rising Motion <term>Motus Attollens; the theory that the entire body of water lifts upward at once</term> or disprove a Progressive Motion <term>Motus in progressu; the theory that the tide is a massive wave moving horizontally across the earth</term>. For it is possible that there is a Progressive Motion of the waters, and yet they nonetheless flood the opposite shores of the same Basin <term>Alveus; literally a channel or "bed," here referring to the Atlantic Ocean basin</term> at the same time, provided that those waters are being thrust and driven from somewhere else. 

This is just like what happens in rivers, which flow up and down both banks at the same hours, even though that movement is clearly a Progressive Motion—specifically, the motion of the waters entering the mouths of the rivers from the sea. Therefore, it could happen in a similar way that waters coming in a great mass from the Eastern Indian Ocean are driven and thrust into the Atlantic Basin, and for that reason flood both sides at once. We must ask, therefore, whether there is another Basin through which the waters can be diminished and ebb at those same times. And the South Sea <note>The Pacific Ocean, commonly referred to in this period as the *Mare Australe* or "South Sea."</note> is right at hand—by no means smaller than the Atlantic, but rather wider and more extensive—which could be sufficient for this purpose.

First, it is evident that the body of water as a whole, as it is placed in the trench or "hollow" of the sea, cannot be raised all at once. This is because there would be no material to take its place at the bottom. Thus, even if there were some kind of "appetite" <note>Bacon often uses the word "appetite" to describe the natural tendency or "desire" of matter to move in a certain way.</note> in the waters to raise themselves, that tendency would be broken and restrained by the "connection of things"—or, as it is commonly phrased, the principle that "nature allows no vacuum" <note>original: *ne detur Vacuum*; the classical belief that space cannot be empty, so water cannot rise unless something else fills the space it left.</note>. It follows, then, that water must be raised in one part and consequently diminished and withdrawn in another. Truly, it follows necessarily that if this magnetic force cannot act upon the whole, it must act most intensely near the middle, raising the waters in the center; as they are lifted, they would successively leave and abandon the sides <note>the coastlines or shores</note>.

And so, we have finally arrived at an <term>Instance of the Cross</term> <note>original: *Instantiam Crucis*; a "fingerpost" or "crucial instance" that stands at a fork in the road to point the way when a researcher must choose between two competing theories.</note> regarding this subject. It is as follows: If it is found that during the ebb tides <note>original: *Refluxibus*; the receding tide.</note> of the sea, the surface of the water is more arched and rounded—that is, with the waters lifting themselves in the middle of the sea and falling away at the sides, which are the shores—and during the flow <note>original: *Fluxibus*; the incoming tide</note> the same surface is flatter and more level as the waters return to their previous position, then certainly, by this **Decisive Instance**, the theory of "Elevation by Magnetic Force" can be accepted; otherwise, it must be rejected entirely.

This is not difficult to test in straits using sounding lines <note>original: *lineas nauticas*; weighted lines used by sailors to measure depth.</note>; namely, to see whether during the ebb, toward the middle of the sea, the water is deeper or more profound than it is during the flow.

Similarly, let the **Nature under Investigation** be that other much-celebrated **Motion of Rotation** <note>original: *Motus Rotationis*</note> among astronomers, which is said to be resisting and contrary to the daily motion—namely, moving from West to East. This is the motion that the ancient astronomers attribute to the planets and even to the starry sky, but which Copernicus and his followers also attribute to the Earth. 

The question to be asked is whether such a motion is actually found in the nature of things, or whether it is instead a thing fabricated and assumed for the sake of shortcuts and the convenience of calculations—and for that beautiful ideal of explaining celestial motions through **perfect circles**. <note>Bacon is skeptical of the long-standing Greek tradition that all heavenly movement must be perfectly circular, a concept that led to very complex mathematical models like epicycles.</note> 

For it is by no means proven that this motion is true and real in the higher heavens, neither by the "failure of return" <note>original: *Defectum Restitutionis*; this refers to the fact that a planet does not return to the exact same spot in the sky relative to the stars after a 24-hour cycle.</note> of a planet in its daily motion to the same point of the starry sky, nor by the different polarity of the Zodiac in respect to the poles of the world. These are the two phenomena that gave birth to this idea of a second motion for us. 

Regarding the first phenomenon: it is best explained by **anticipation** <note>original: *Anteversionem*</note> and **lagging behind** <note>original: *Derelictionem*</note>. Regarding the second: it is better explained by **spiral lines**. <note>Bacon suggests that instead of two different rotations pulling in opposite directions, there is only one daily motion, but planets move at different speeds or in spiral paths rather than perfect circles.</note> The result is that the inequality of a planet's return and its declination toward the tropics may be seen as modifications of that single daily motion, rather than as motions that resist each other or move around different poles. 

And it is most certain—if we behave for a moment like common folk, setting aside the fictions of the astronomers and the Schools <note>The "Schools" refers to the Scholastic tradition of the universities, which Bacon often criticized for being too theoretical and disconnected from physical observation.</note> (whose habit it is to do violence to the senses in many ways and to prefer more obscure explanations)—that such a motion appears to the senses exactly as we have described it.

### XXXVIII.

Next follow five classes of *Instances*, which we are accustomed to call by the single general name *Instances of the Lamp* <note>original: "Instantias Lampadis"</note>, or of *Primary Information*. These are the ones that assist the Senses. Since every *Interpretation of Nature* begins with the Senses, and leads from the perceptions of the Senses—by a straight, steady, and fortified path—to the perceptions of the Intellect (which are true <term>Notions</term> <note>meaning: fundamental concepts or ideas</note> and <term>Axioms</term> <note>meaning: established principles or laws of nature</note>), it follows that the more abundant and exact the representations or presentations of the Senses are, the more easily and successfully everything will proceed.

Of these five *Instances of the Lamp*:
1. The First strengthen, enlarge, and rectify the immediate actions of the Senses. 
2. The Second bring the <term>non-Sensible</term> <note>things that cannot be directly perceived, such as atoms or hidden forces</note> to the Sensible. 
3. The Third indicate the continuous progresses or Series of those things and motions which (for the most part) are not noticed except at their conclusion or after certain periods. 
4. The Fourth substitute something for the Senses when they are utterly failing <note>providing a proxy or indirect measurement when a sense cannot detect anything at all</note>. 
5. The Fifth excite the attention and notice of the Senses, and at the same time limit the subtlety <note>the fine, complex details</note> of things. 

We must now speak of each of these individually.

XXXIX.
**A**mong the *Prerogative Instances* <note>Bacon uses the term "Prerogative Instances" to describe specific types of observations or experiments that are more valuable than others because they provide "privileged" information that speeds up the discovery of truth.</note>, we shall place in the sixteenth position the *Instances of the Door or Gate*: for that is the name we give to those things which assist the immediate actions of the Senses. Among the Senses, it is manifest that Sight holds the primary place regarding information; therefore, aids for this Sense are especially to be sought. These aids seem to be of three kinds: either to perceive things not seen; or to see at a greater distance; or to see more exactly and distinctly.

Of the first kind (setting aside Spectacles and similar things, which serve only to correct and relieve the weakness of a poorly functioning Sight, and thus provide no further information) are those recently invented Perspective Glasses <note>original: "Perspicilla". Furthermore, they say that a straight line drawn with a pen or brush appears quite uneven and crooked through these Perspective Glasses; because, of course, neither the motion of the hand (even if guided by a ruler) nor the application of the ink or color is truly even.

->XI.<-

**Among** the Prerogative Instances <term>Prerogative Instances: Bacon’s term for specific types of data or observations that hold special "privileges" or power in guiding an investigation toward the truth.</term> we shall place in the seventeenth position **Summoning Instances**; taking the term from the Civil Courts, because they summon things to appear that previously have not appeared: we have also been accustomed to call these **Evoking Instances**. However, things escape the senses either because of the distance of the object’s location; or because the sense is blocked by intervening bodies; or because the object is not fit to make an impression on the sense; or because there is a deficiency in the **Quantity** of the object to strike the sense; or because the **Time** is not proportioned to activate the sense; or because the striking of the object is not tolerated by the sense <note>For example, a light so bright it blinds or a sound so loud it deafens.</note>; or because the object has previously filled and possessed the sense, so that there is no room for a new motion. These limitations pertain especially to Sight, and secondarily to Touch. For these two senses provide information broadly and regarding "Common Objects"; whereas the remaining three senses hardly provide information at all except immediately and regarding their "Proper Objects." <note>In classical philosophy, "Common Objects" (sensibilia communia) are things like shape, number, and motion which can be perceived by multiple senses. ### XLI.

Among the **Prerogative Instances** <note>Bacon uses this term to describe "privileged" or particularly useful types of evidence that have a "prerogative" (a special right) to guide our understanding over others.</note>, we will place in the eighteenth position the **Instances of the Way**; which we are also accustomed to call **Traveling Instances**, or **Articulated Instances** <note>original: "Instantias Articulatas." This refers to processes broken down into distinct stages or "joints."</note>. These are the ones which indicate the motions of Nature as they continue step by step.

This kind of instance, however, escapes observation rather than the senses themselves. For there is a remarkable lack of diligence among men regarding this matter. Indeed, they contemplate Nature only fitfully and at intervals, and only after bodies have been finished and completed, rather than during their actual operation. If someone desired to explore and contemplate the skill and industry of any craftsman, he would not only wish to see the raw materials of the craft and then the finished works; instead, he would prefer to be present while the craftsman is working and advancing his project.

A similar approach must be taken regarding Nature. For example, if someone inquires into the growth of plants, he must inspect it from the very sowing of a seed. This can easily be done by digging up seeds—almost daily—that have remained in the earth for two, three, four days, and so on, and by a diligent inspection of them. One should observe how and when the seed begins to swell and grow turgid, and as if filled with spirit <note>original: "veluti spiritu impleri." In 17th-century science, "spirits" were thought to be active, invisible substances that triggered biological growth and movement.</note>; then how it begins to break its skin and put forth...

Similarly, there is no Body found here among us that does not take in Heat when brought near a fire. Yet, Air receives heat far more quickly than Stone. And such is the **Substitution** which is made by **Degrees**.

But **Substitution by Analogs** is certainly useful, yet it is less certain; and for that reason, it must be applied with a specific judgment. This occurs when something <term>Non-sensible</term> <note>original: "Non-sensibile"; things that cannot be directly perceived by the human senses, such as the internal "spirits" of matter.</note> is brought to the Senses; not through the sensible operations of the invisible body itself, but through the contemplation of some related Sensible Body. For example: if an inquiry is made into the **Mixture of Spirits**, which are non-visible bodies; there seems to be a certain kinship between Bodies and their Fuels or Nourishment. The fuel of Flame appears to be Oil and Fatty substances; that of Air, Water and Watery substances: for Flames multiply themselves upon the fumes of Oil, and Air multiplies itself upon the vapors of Water.

We call the three instances belonging to this category by the single name *Propitious* or *Benevolent Instances*. And it is certain that thinner bodies (such as air) undergo a notable contraction, as has been said; but tangible bodies (such as water) undergo compression much more reluctantly and into a smaller space. We investigated the degree of compression they might suffer through the following experiment.

We had a hollow globe made of lead, which could contain about two <term>wine pints</term> <note>original: "pintas vinarias." A standard liquid measure; in 17th-century England, this would be roughly 0.94 liters.</note>; and its walls were thick enough to withstand a greater force. We poured water into it through a hole made in one spot; and that hole, after the globe had been filled with water, we stopped up with melted lead, so that the globe became entirely sealed. Then, with a heavy hammer, we flattened the globe on two opposite sides; as a result, the water was necessarily forced into a smaller space, since the <term>sphere</term> is the most capacious of shapes <note>original: "cum Sphæra Figurarum sit capacissima." This refers to the geometric principle that a sphere has the largest volume for a given surface area; any deformation of the sphere reduces its internal volume.</note>. Next, when the hammering no longer sufficed, as the water yielded more reluctantly, we used a mill or a press; until finally the water, unable to endure further pressure, began to sweat through the solid lead like a delicate dew. Afterwards, we calculated how much space had been reduced by that compression; and we understood that the water had undergone a compression of that amount (though only when subjected to great force).

->### XLVI.<-

Among the **Prerogative Instances** <note>Bacon's "Prerogative Instances" are specific types of evidence or experiments that provide more information than others and should be prioritized in scientific study.</note> we shall place in the twenty-second position the **Instances of the Course**, which we are also accustomed to call **Instances of the Water**; taking the name from the <term>water-clocks<note>original: "Clepsydris"</note></term> used by the ancients, into which water was poured instead of sand. First, therefore, we see that the **revolutions** of the **celestial bodies** occur through measured periods of time; as do the **ebb and flow of the sea**. The downward motion of **heavy objects** toward the Earth, and of **light objects** toward the circumference of the heavens, occurs through certain moments <note>Bacon uses "momenta" to mean specific increments or durations of time</note>, according to the ratio of the body being moved and the medium through which it travels. Furthermore, the sailing of ships, the movements of animals, and the flight of projectiles all happen likewise through spans of time that (taken in total) can be numbered.

Concerning **heat**, indeed, we see that boys during winter may wash their hands in flames and yet not be burnt; <note>original: "manus in flamma lavare." This refers to a common trick where quick movement prevents the skin from reaching a damaging temperature.</note> and performers turn vessels full of wine or water upside down with agile and steady motions, and then recover them right side up without spilling the liquid; and many things of this sort. No less do the **compressions**, **expansions**, and **eruptions** of bodies occur—some faster, some slower—according to the nature of the body and its motion, but always through certain moments of time.

### XLVII.

Among the **Prerogative Instances** <note>Bacon's "Prerogative Instances" are specific types of examples or experiments that have a special power to reveal the truth of nature</note>, we shall place in the twenty-third position the **Instances of Quantity**, which we have been accustomed to call the **Doses of Nature** (borrowing the term from medicine). XLVIII.
Among the *Prerogative Instances* <note>Bacon's "Prerogative Instances" are specific types of evidence or observations that have "special rights" or higher priority in scientific inquiry because they reveal the inner workings of nature more clearly than common experience.</note>, we place in the twenty-fourth position the *Instances of Strife*; which we have also been accustomed to call *Instances of Predominance*. In this context, it refers to the inherent capacities or forces of a substance, not moral virtue.</note> over one another; showing which among them is stronger and wins out, and which is weaker and gives way. For the Motions and Strivings of bodies are composed, decomposed, and complicated, no less than the Bodies themselves. We shall therefore first propose the primary Species of Motions or Active Powers, so that the comparison of their respective Strength may be clearer, and from there, the Demonstration and Definition of the *Instances of Strife and Predominance*.

The first motion is the Motion of the *Resistance of Matter* <term>original Latin: *Antitypiæ Materiæ*. From the Greek "antitypia," meaning "to strike back." Thus, no fire, no weight or pressure, no violence, and finally no age or length of time can reduce even the smallest portion of Matter to Nothing; rather, it will always be Something, and occupy some Space, and (whatever necessity it is placed in) it will defend itself either by changing its Form or

Therefore, the matter is not reduced to *Penetration of dimensions* and *vacuum*, except at the extreme limits of Condensation and Rarefaction. However, these motions stop and operate far short of those limits; they are nothing more than the Desires of Bodies to preserve themselves in their Consistencies (or, if they prefer, in their Forms), and not to depart from them suddenly, unless they are altered through gentle means and by mutual consent.

# Chapter V

## ->On the Laws of Nature<-

The law of nature is a dictate of right reason <note>In the 17th century, "right reason" referred to the human capacity to understand the moral order of the universe through logic and intellect.</note> pointing out that an action, depending on its agreement or disagreement with rational nature, possesses a quality of moral necessity or moral turpitude. Its primary aim is the **preservation of life** and the avoidance of what is destructive to it.

<margin>Hobbes in *Leviathan*</margin>

From this it follows that peace is to be sought, as far as there is hope of obtaining it. When a man cannot obtain peace, he may seek and use all helps and advantages of war. This arises because in the "state of nature," there exists <note>original: "jus omnium in omnia"</note> a **right of everyone to everything**, even to one another's bodies, which leads only to perpetual conflict and fear.

The second law is: That a man be willing, when others are so too <insert>provided that others do the same</insert>, to lay down this right to all things; and be contented with so much liberty against other men as he would allow other men against himself. This transition is achieved <gloss>that is, by the renunciation of one's rights</gloss> through a mutual agreement.

| Law | Action Required |
| :--- | :--- |
| **Law I** | Peace must be sought |
| **Law II** | Rights must be surrendered |

By this transfer of right, a person is said to be obliged or bound not to hinder those to whom such right is granted. This surrender of individual power forms the basis of what is known as the <term>Social Contract</term> <note>The Social Contract is the political and moral theory that individuals give up certain natural freedoms to a central authority in exchange for the protection of their remaining rights and the maintenance of social order.</note>. Without this mutual agreement, no security is possible, and the life of man remains solitary, poor, and short.

<summary>This page outlines the first two "Laws of Nature" based on the philosophy of Thomas Hobbes, explaining how the rational need for self-preservation leads humans to seek peace and surrender their absolute rights.</summary>
<keywords>natural law, Thomas Hobbes, right reason, peace, social contract, self-preservation, Leviathan</keywords>

But the motion of **Excitation** proceeds as if by art and insinuation, and stealthily; it only invites and disposes the excited thing toward the nature of the exciter. Also, the motion of **Assimilation** multiplies and transforms bodies and substances; for example, more flame is produced, more air, more <term>spirit</term><note>In 17th-century science, "spirit" refers to subtle, active, gas-like substances trapped within solid matter that drive physical changes.</note>, and more flesh.

Thus, heat is excited much more slowly and with greater difficulty in stone or metal than in air, due to the inability and unreadiness of those bodies for that specific motion. If the weight is [greater], it yields. A lever of such strength will lift such a weight; up to that point, the *Motion of Liberty* <term>Motus Libertatis: The tendency of a body to resist being compressed or stretched and to return to its original state.</term> dominates over the *Motion of the Greater Congregation* <term>Motus Congregationis majoris: The force we now call gravity, which pulls objects toward the center of the earth.</term>; but if the weight is greater, it yields. # 348 &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;OF VERULAM <note>Francis Bacon held the title Baron Verulam.</note>

On the outer surfaces, a most useful practice is the pouring of oil over wine or the juices of herbs; by spreading itself across the top like a lid, it preserves them perfectly from being harmed by the **Air**. In a similar way, we must look carefully to see if there are any *Substitutes for Cold*; namely, by what methods <term>Condensations</term> <note>the process of making a substance denser or more solid</note> can be produced in bodies by means other than the cold that usually performs this as its own particular work. These condensations seem to be contained within four methods (as far as is yet clear).

The first of these seems to be done by simple *Compression*: which has little power to create a lasting density (for bodies spring back <note>Bacon is observing elasticity; most materials return to their original volume after being squeezed</note>), but nonetheless it might perhaps be a helpful auxiliary tool. 

The second occurs by the *Contraction* of the thicker parts in a body after the evaporation or escape of the thinner parts, as happens in the hardening of materials by fire, and the repeated quenching of metals, and similar processes. 

The third occurs by the *Union* <note>original: *Coitionem*; a coming together or gathering</note> of the "homogeneous" parts (parts of the same kind) which are the most solid in a body, and which had previously been dispersed and mixed with less solid parts. For example, in the restoration of *Sublimated Mercury* <note>a chemical compound of mercury; when reduced back to its pure liquid state, it becomes much denser</note>, which in powder form occupies a far greater space than simple mercury; and similarly in every refining of metals from their dross <note>original: *Scoriis*; the stony waste matter separated from metals during smelting</note>. 

The fourth occurs by *Sympathies* <note>original: *Consensus*; Bacon refers to "agreements" or natural attractions between specific substances that cause them to react</note>, by applying things which condense through the hidden power of bodies. These "sympathies" have so far rarely shown themselves; which is not at all surprising, because until the discovery of *Forms* <note>the fundamental "laws" or "blueprints" of nature in Bacon's philosophy</note> and -ing Sche- <note>the text breaks off mid-word, likely heading toward *Schematismus*, or the hidden "structural configurations" of matter</note>

<summary>Bacon explores four methods of condensing matter without using cold: physical pressure, evaporation of light parts, the gathering of solid particles, and chemical "sympathies." This is part of his larger effort to master the physical properties of materials through experimental science.</summary>

# NOVUM ORGANUM. 369

...Magical Instances. <note>original: "Instantias Magicas". For Bacon, "Magical" does not mean supernatural; it refers to natural phenomena where a very small cause produces a massive, seemingly miraculous effect.</note> We call them by this name—those cases in which the **Matter** or the **Efficient Cause** <term>Efficient Cause|The immediate agent or "trigger" that brings a change into being</term> is slight or small compared to the magnitude of the Work and the Effect that follows; so much so that even if they were common, they would still be like a Miracle—some at first glance, others even to one observing more closely. Nature herself provides these sparingly; but what she will accomplish once her secrets are shaken out <note>Latin: "sinu excusso," a metaphor meaning to search or empty out the hidden folds of a garment</note>, and after the discovery of **Forms**, **Processes**, and **Configurations** <term>Schematisms|The hidden internal structures or arrangements of the smallest particles within a body</term>, will appear in future times.

But those **Magical Effects** (as far as we can yet guess) happen in three ways:
*   Either by the **Multiplication of themselves**; as in Fire, and in those poisons called **Specifics** <note>Substances thought to act with high potency on specific organs or through unique properties</note>; and also in Motions that are passed along and strengthened from **Wheel to Wheel** <note>Referring to the mechanical advantage and force amplification in geared machinery</note>.
*   Or by **Excitation** or **Invitation** in another; as in the **Magnet**, which excites [magnetizes] countless needles without its own power being in any way lost or diminished; or in **leaven** <note>yeast</note>, and things of this sort.
*   Or by the **Pre-emption of Motion** <note>original: "Anteversionem Motus", the sudden, accelerated release of energy</note>, as was said regarding **Gunpowder**, **Cannons**, and **Mines** <note>Military tunnels packed with explosives used to blow up fortifications</note>.

## LII.
AND so, let these things be said concerning the Dignities or *Prerogatives of Instances*. <note>Bacon refers to "Prerogative Instances" as specific types of data or observations that hold more weight or "privilege" when trying to understand a law of nature.</note> It must be warned, however, that in this *Organon* <note>original: "Organo" — meaning an instrument or tool; here referring to his book, the *Novum Organum*.</note> of ours, we are treating Logic, not Philosophy. **T**he reason we are publishing our *Great Renewal* <note>original: *Instaurationem nostram*. This refers to Bacon’s "Instauratio Magna," his grand plan to reorganize all human knowledge.</note> in parts is to ensure that at least some of it is placed beyond the reach of risk. A similar reason moves us to append another small portion of the work at this time, publishing it alongside those parts we have already completed. This portion is a Description and Delineation of a Natural and Experimental History—specifically, the kind of history required to build a sound Philosophy. It must contain material that is reliable, abundant, and properly organized for the work of the *Interpreter* <note>Bacon refers to the "Interpreter of Nature," the scientist who uses his specific method of induction to decode the laws of the universe.</note> which follows.

The proper place for this discussion would have been when our systematic inquiry reached the *Preparations* <note>original: *Parascevas*, a Greek term meaning a preamble or a stage of preparation.</note>. However, it seems more prudent to address it now rather than waiting for its strictly logical place. This is because a History of the kind we envision—and will soon describe—is an undertaking of immense scale. It cannot be completed without great effort and expense, requiring the labor of many people; indeed, as we have remarked elsewhere, it is a task fit for a King <note>original: *opus sit quasi Regium*</note>. Therefore, it occurred to us that it might be useful to share this plan now, in case others might take up the cause. This way, while we—

We have become accustomed to calling this history the *Primary History*, or the *Mother History*.

For this reason it happens that Astronomy, Optics, Music, many Mechanical Arts, and even Medicine itself, and (what might surprise one more) Moral and Civil Philosophy, and the Logical Sciences, have almost no depth in their foundations; but instead only glide along the surface and variety of things: because after these particular Sciences were divided and established, they were no longer nourished by Natural Philosophy; which could have imparted new strength and growth to them from the sources and true contemplations of Motions, Rays, Sounds, the Texture and **Configuration** <note>original: "Schematismi"—a technical term Bacon uses to describe the internal arrangement of parts in a body</note> of Bodies, **Passions** <note>original: "Affectuum"—here meaning the physical properties or "impressions" of matter, not just human emotions</note>, and Intellectual perceptions. Therefore, it is not at all surprising if the Sciences do not grow, since they are separated from their roots.

These thinkers are only anxious that their own **Art** be considered perfect, devoting themselves to a most vain and ruinous glory—namely, that whatever has not yet been discovered and understood should be believed to be altogether impossible to discover or understand in the future.

This refers to the mapping of stars or the astronomical configuration of the sky.</note>, and similar things which seem to contain some hidden secret,

<summary>Francis Bacon argues that scholars often claim things are "impossible" simply because their current methods have failed, creating a "malicious despair" that discourages new scientific discovery. He criticizes those who focus on single mysteries like magnetism rather than seeking a broader understanding of the natural world.</summary>

Take, for instance, the nature of **Consistency** <note>In this context, Bacon is referring to "cohesion" or the property of matter staying together.</note>, which is not noticed in wood or stone, but is passed over under the name of "solid," and no further inquiry is made into why it avoids separation or the <term>breaking of continuity</term> <note>original: *solutionis continuitatis*; a phrase often used in early science to describe the physical parting of a substance.</note>. And indeed, those very things which are considered "secrets" possess in other things a manifest and common nature; yet this nature will never reveal itself to be seen if men's experiments or contemplations are focused only on those secret things themselves. 

Generally and commonly, in mechanical works, things are considered "new inventions" if someone merely refines existing inventions more delicately, or decorates them more elegantly, or joins and composes them together, or links them more conveniently for use, or presents a work in a larger or even smaller mass or volume than was customary, and similar things.
