### LXXXIX.

Nor should we overlook the fact that <term>Natural Philosophy: The historical name for the study of nature and the physical universe; the precursor to modern science</term> has, in every age, encountered a troublesome and difficult adversary: namely, Superstition and a blind, immoderate zeal for Religion. For we see among the Greeks that those who first proposed natural causes for lightning and storms to ears as yet unaccustomed were condemned for impiety against the gods on that account. Nor were those treated much better by some of the ancient <term>Church Fathers: Influential Christian teachers and theologians from the first few centuries of the Church</term> of the Christian religion, who, based on the most certain proofs (which no sane person today would dispute), proposed that the Earth is round and consequently asserted the existence of the <term>Antipodes: People living on the opposite side of the globe</term>.

Furthermore, in the present state of affairs, the conditions for discussing Nature have become even harsher and more dangerous due to the "Summas" <note>original: "Summas" — Reference to the "Summa Theologica" and similar comprehensive medieval theological textbooks</note> and methods of the <term>Scholastic: Medieval university scholars who sought to reconcile Christian doctrine with classical Greek philosophy</term> theologians. These men, having reduced Theology to a strict order as far as they were able and shaped it into the form of a formal discipline, have additionally ensured that the contentious and thorny philosophy of *Aristotle* is joined to the Body <note>The sentence ends abruptly as the page breaks; it likely concludes "to the Body of the Church" or "to the Body of Scripture" on the following page.</note>

<summary>Bacon argues that "Natural Philosophy" (science) has been historically hindered by religious superstition and the rigid, Aristotelian methods adopted by medieval Scholastic theologians.</summary>

...wise and serious men in these matters tend to utterly despair. Because of this, they believe that the sciences experience certain ebbs and flows <note>original: "fluxus & refluxus"</note> throughout the revolutions of time and the ages of the world. And since these are the kinds of thoughts that easily occur to serious men of excellent judgment, we must truly take care that we do not relax or diminish the severity of our judgment, even if we are captivated by the love of a most excellent and beautiful goal. We must carefully examine what hope shines forth, and from what direction it reveals itself. Once the lighter breezes of hope have been rejected, we must thoroughly discuss and weigh those reasons that seem to have more firmness.

### XCIII.

The beginning must be taken from God: specifically, that this work which is at hand, because of the excellent nature of the Good within it, is clearly from God, who is the **Author of Good** and the **Father of lights.** <note>original: "Pater luminum"; a biblical reference to James 1:17, common in Bacon’s writing to link scientific discovery with divine enlightenment.</note> In divine operations, even the smallest beginnings lead surely to their end. And what was said of spiritual matters—*The Kingdom of God does not come with observation* <note>original: "Regnum Dei non venit cum observatione"; Luke 17:20. Bacon suggests that major shifts in human history often happen quietly before they are noticed.</note>—is also found to happen in every major work of divine Providence: so that everything glides forward peacefully without noise or clatter, and the thing is fully underway before people realize or notice it is happening. 

Nor should we omit the prophecy of *Daniel* regarding the last times of the world: *Many shall pass through, and knowledge shall be increased.* <note>original: "Multi pertransibunt, & multiplex erit scientia"; Daniel 12:4. This was the motto on the frontispiece of the Novum Organum, famously depicted as a ship sailing past the Pillars of Hercules.</note> This clearly hints and signifies that it is in the Fates—that is, in Providence—that the circumnavigation of the world (which is fully accomplished by so many long voyages, or at least seems now in progress) and the growth of the <term>Sciences</term> <note>Latin "Scientiarum" here refers to systematic knowledge and discovery of the natural world.</note> should occur in the same age.

### XCIV.

Next follows the greatest reason of all for creating hope; namely, from the errors of time past and the paths attempted thus far. For the best rebuke is that which someone once phrased regarding a State not wisely governed: *What is worst regarding the past, is best regarding the future.* <note>original: "Quod ad præterita pessimum est, id ad futura optimum"; Bacon is quoting the Greek orator Demosthenes. The logic is that if we had tried everything and still failed, there would be no hope; but if we failed because we used the wrong methods, then changing the methods provides a reason for hope.</note>

### XCVIII.
The foundations of **Experience** (since we must eventually arrive there) have been either non-existent or extremely weak up to this point. Neither a <term>forest</term> <note>original: *sylva*. Bacon uses this term to refer to a "timber-yard" or a raw mass of data—a collection of facts that have not yet been refined into scientific laws.</note> nor a body of material regarding **Particulars**—adequate in its number, variety, or certainty to inform the human Understanding—has yet been sought out or gathered together. 

On the contrary, learned men (who are, truth be told, quite lazy and careless) have accepted certain rumors of experience—mere whispers and echoes of it—to either build or bolster their philosophy. Despite the poor quality of this information, they have granted these rumors the weight of legitimate evidence. 

It is as if a Kingdom or State were to manage its affairs and councils not by official letters and reports sent from trustworthy **Ambassadors** and **Messengers**, but rather by the idle gossip of city-dwellers and the chatter of the streets. Such is the "administration" that has been introduced into Philosophy regarding Experience. In the study of <term>Natural History</term> <note>In the 17th century, "Natural History" meant a systematic catalog of all natural facts, observations, and experiments, rather than just the study of plants and animals.</note>, nothing is found that has been properly investigated, nothing verified, nothing counted, nothing weighed, and nothing measured. And whatever is indefinite and vague in observation must necessarily be deceptive and untrustworthy when used for instruction.

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; ## CI.

Once a sufficient supply and store of Natural History and Experience—the kind required for the work of the Intellect, or for the work of Philosophy—is ready and at hand, the Intellect is still by no means capable of acting on that material spontaneously and by memory alone. ->### CIII.<-

**BUT** once a wealth of particulars <note>In this context, "particulars" refers to individual observations, data points, or specific instances of a phenomenon.</note> has been properly and orderly placed before our eyes, we must not immediately leap to investigating and discovering new particulars or practical works. For indeed, the **lowest Axioms** do not differ much from bare **Experience**. But those **supreme** and **most general** ones (as they are currently held) are merely conceptual and abstract, and possess no solidity. However, the **middle Axioms** are those which are true, solid, and living, upon which human affairs and fortunes depend; and above these, finally, are those very general ones; such, that is, which are not abstract, but are truly defined and limited by these middle axioms.

Therefore, the human **Intellect** should not be given **feathers**, but rather **lead** and **weights**, to restrain all leaping and flying. This has not yet been done; but when it is done, we will be permitted to hope for better things from the **Sciences**.

### CV.

In establishing an <term>Axiom</term> <note>original: "Axiomate." In Bacon's work, an axiom is a general law or principle derived from observing nature, not just a self-evident truth.</note>, however, a form of *Induction* different from what has been in use until now must be devised; and this should be applied not only to proving and discovering "First Principles" (as they call them), but also to the lesser axioms, the middle axioms, and indeed, all of them. For that Induction which proceeds by "simple enumeration" <note>original: "enumerationem simplicem." This refers to the old method of drawing a general conclusion simply because no counter-example has been noticed yet.</note> is a childish thing; it concludes precariously and is exposed to the danger of a contradictory instance. It usually passes judgment based on fewer instances than is proper, and only from those facts which are close at hand. 

But the *Induction* which will be useful for the discovery and demonstration of Sciences and Arts must separate Nature through proper rejections and exclusions; and then, after a sufficient number of negatives have been established, it must reach a conclusion on the affirmatives. This has not yet been done, nor even certainly attempted, except perhaps by *Plato*, who uses this form of Induction to some extent for the purpose of examining definitions and ideas. 

Truly, for the good and lawful instruction of this Induction (or Demonstration), many more things must be employed than have ever entered the thoughts of any mortal man; so much so, that more labor must be spent on this than has been spent on the <term>Syllogism</term> <note>A traditional form of logic where a conclusion is drawn from two premises (e.g., All men are mortal; Socrates is a man; therefore Socrates is mortal). Bacon felt this was useless for discovering new scientific truths.</note> up to this point. And with the help of this Induction, we must use it not only for discovering Axioms, but also for defining <insert>clear</insert> Notions...

<summary>Bacon introduces his "New Induction," arguing that science should not just list examples but must systematically exclude false possibilities to find the truth, a much harder task than traditional logic.</summary>

### CVI.

->NOVUM ORGANUM. 119<-

The human mind, in this pursuit of discovery, is often so awkward and poorly disposed that it first lacks confidence, and shortly after despises itself. At first, it seems incredible to the mind that any such thing could be found; yet after it has been discovered, it seems incredible again that mankind could have missed it for so long. These can be derived not only from digging out unknown operations, but also by transferring and applying those already known through what we call <term>Literate Experience<note>original: "Experientiam literatam"; Bacon's term for a systematic, written-down method of experimenting that leads from one experiment to another, as opposed to "vague experience" or mere trial and error.</note></term>.

### CXIV.

Lastly, even if a much weaker and more obscure breeze of Hope should blow from that *new Continent* <note>original: "nova Continente"; Bacon frequently uses the recent discovery of the Americas as a metaphor for the undiscovered truths of the natural world</note>; we have nevertheless determined that the attempt must absolutely be made (unless we wish to be utterly dejected in spirit). For the risk of not making an attempt is not equal to the risk of an attempt failing. In the former case, we lose the chance at a massive benefit; in the latter, we only waste a small amount of human labor. Indeed, from what has been said, and even from what has been left unsaid, it seems to us that there is abundant ground for hope—not only for the vigorous man to try the experiment, but even for the prudent and sober man to believe in its success.

### CXV.

And so, we have now finished speaking about the removal of despair, which has been among the most powerful causes for delaying and inhibiting the progress of the Sciences. At the same time, we have concluded our discussion of the Signs <note>Bacon refers to the "signs" or omens that current philosophies are failing and that his new method is promising.</note>...

### CXIX.
There will also appear in our **Natural History** <note>A "Natural History" in Bacon's time was not just about biology, but a systematic encyclopedia of all observed facts and phenomena in nature.</note> and **Experiments** many things; first, those that are trivial and common; next, those that are base and unrefined; and finally, those that are overly subtle and purely speculative, appearing to be of no use. This is the kind of material that might turn away and alienate the interest of men.

But regarding those things which seem common, let men consider this: that they have hitherto been accustomed to do nothing else but explain the causes of rare events by referring them to things that happen frequently. However, they seek no causes for the things that happen frequently themselves, but simply accept them as granted and self-evident.

Therefore, they do not seek the causes of **Weight**, of the **Rotation of the Heavenly Bodies**, of **Heat**, **Cold**, **Light**, **Hardness**, **Softness**, **Thinness**, **Density**, **Liquidity**, **Consistency**, of the **Animate** <note>original: "Animati," referring to living things or those possessed of a soul/life-force.</note>, the **Inanimate**, the **Similar**, the **Dissimilar**, or finally of **Organic Structure**. Instead, they accept these things as obvious and manifest, and then use them to dispute and judge other matters which do not occur so frequently or familiarly.

We, however, know well enough that no judgment can be made concerning rare or notable things—much less can new things be brought to light—without first examining the causes of common things, and the causes of those causes...

### CXXVI.

## II.

How unhappy the state of the human science currently in use is, may be seen even from those things commonly asserted. It is rightly established that: *To truly know is to know through causes.* Likewise, the four Causes <note>Bacon is referencing Aristotle’s four causes: Material (what it's made of), Formal (its essence/design), Efficient (the agent that makes it), and Final (its purpose).</note> are not badly defined: Matter, Form, Efficient, and Final. As for the Efficient cause and Matter (at least in the way they are sought and accepted—that is, as distant causes, without investigating the *latent process* that leads to the form), these are perfunctory and superficial matters, and of almost no value for a true and active science. <meta>This page continues Section II of Book II of Francis Bacon's Novum Organum (The New Organon), where he defines the relationship between individual bodies and the universal "Forms" or laws of nature.</meta>

146 ->[LORD] VERULAM<-

...yet we have not forgotten that we noted and corrected above the error of the human mind in assigning the primary place of essence to <term>Forms</term> <note>In traditional philosophy, a "Form" was an abstract essence; Bacon redefines it here as the objective physical law that governs a quality like heat or light.</note>. For although in Nature nothing truly exists except individual bodies, performing pure individual acts according to a law; yet in science, that very law—including its investigation, discovery, and explanation—serves as the foundation for both knowing and doing. By the name of **Forms**, we understand this law and its specific clauses, especially since this term has become established and is commonly encountered.

### III.

One who knows the **Cause** of any nature (such as whiteness or heat) in only certain subjects has imperfect knowledge. Likewise, one who can only produce an effect upon certain specific materials (among those capable of receiving it) has an equally imperfect power. 

But he who knows only the <term>Efficient</term> <note>The immediate agent or force that triggers a change.</note> and <term>Material</term> <note>The physical matter that undergoes a change.</note> causes (which are fleeting causes, nothing more than vehicles that convey the Form in certain instances) may reach new inventions in materials that are somewhat similar and already prepared; however, he does not shift the more deeply fixed boundaries of things. 

But he who knows **Forms** embraces the unity of Nature in the most dissimilar materials. ### VIII.

Nor will this investigation lead us to the <term>Atom</term> <note>Bacon rejects the "Atomism" of thinkers like Democritus, which required the existence of a vacuum.</note>, which presupposes a Vacuum and matter that does not flow (both of which are false). ### IX.
From the two kinds of Axioms <note>Bacon previously distinguished between axioms of variable instances and axioms of fixed laws.</note> which were set out above, there arises a true division of Philosophy and the sciences; by adapting the received terms (which come closest to indicating the matter) to our own meaning. The former, however, is divided into three parts; namely into three Ministrations: Ministration to the Senses, Ministration to the Memory, and Ministration to the Mind, or Reason.

### XII.

**Second**, a presentation must be made to the **Understanding** of **Instances** <note>technical term for specific examples or cases used in an argument</note> which are deprived of the **given Nature**: because the **Form** <note>In Bacon’s philosophy, the "Form" is the internal law or essential nature that makes a thing what it is.</note> (as has been said) must be no less absent where the given nature is absent, than present where it is present. This, however, would be an infinite task in all cases.

Therefore, **Negatives** must be subjoined to **Affirmatives**, and **Privations** <note>the absence or lack of a quality</note> must be inspected only in those **Subjects** which are most closely related to those others in which the given nature is present and appears. This we are accustomed to call the **Table of Deviation**, or **Absence in Proximity**.

->**Instances in proximity which are deprived of the nature of Heat.**<-

->**To the first Affirmative Instance.**<-

The rays of the **Moon**, **Stars**, and **Comets** are not found to be hot to the touch; indeed, the sharpest colds are usually observed during **Full Moons**.

->**First Negative or Subjunctive Instance.**<-

But the larger **fixed Stars**, when the **Sun** passes under them or approaches them, are thought to increase and intensify the **Sun's** heat; as happens when the **Sun** stays in **Leo**, and during the **Dog Days**. <note>original: "Diebus Canicularibus." The hottest days of summer, historically associated with the rising of the star Sirius, the "Dog Star."</note>

### Regarding the second table, the second instance.

The rays of the Sun in the "Middle Region of the Air" (as they call it) do not produce heat. The reason commonly given for this is quite sensible: that this region is neither close enough to the body of the Sun, from which the rays emanate, nor to the Earth, from which they are reflected. <note>Bacon refers to the traditional Aristotelian meteorology which divided the atmosphere into three regions; the middle region was thought to be naturally cold because it was distant from both the sun and the "rebound" of heat from the earth’s surface.</note> And this is evident from the summits of mountains (unless they are extremely high), where snow lasts perpetually. 

But, on the contrary, it has been noted by some that on the peak of the *Peak of Tenerife*, and also in the *Peruvian Andes*, the very summits of the mountains are free from snow, while the snow lies only lower down during the ascent. <note>Tenerife is the largest of the Canary Islands; its volcanic peak, Teide, was a frequent point of reference for early modern scientists.</note> Moreover, the air on those very mountain peaks is found to be not cold at all, but only thin and sharp. Indeed, in the *Andes*, this air is so sharp that it stings and wounds the eyes through its excessive acrimony, and even stings the upper opening of the stomach, causing vomiting. <note>Bacon is describing the effects of high altitude and low oxygen, which he interprets as "acrimony" or "thinness" of the air.</note> 

It was also noted by the Ancients that on the summit of *Mount Olympus* the thinness of the air was so great that those who climbed it found it necessary to carry sponges soaked in vinegar and water, applying them periodically to the mouth and nose; this was because the air, due to its thinness, was insufficient for breathing. It was also reported that on this same summit there was such serenity and peace from rain, snow, and winds, that for those performing sacrifices, letters traced with a finger in the ashes of the sacrifices upon the altar of *Jupiter* remained until the following year without any disturbance. <note>This anecdote from antiquity was used to suggest that the highest peaks reached above the "turbulent" part of the atmosphere into a region of perfect stillness.</note>

*Regarding the second point, the third observation.*
The reflection of the sun's rays in regions near the Polar Circles is found to be quite weak and ineffective in producing heat. So much so that the Dutch, who spent the winter in *Nova Zembla* <note>original: "nova Zembla"; refers to Novaya Zemlya, an Arctic archipelago where explorer Willem Barentsz was famously stranded in 1596</note>, while they were waiting for the release and clearing of their ship from the mass of ice (which had besieged it), were frustrated in their hope even by the beginning of July, and were forced to commit themselves to a small boat. Thus, direct rays of the sun seem to have little power, even on flat ground; nor do the reflected rays, unless they are multiplied and united. This happens when the sun moves closer to the perpendicular <note>i.e., directly overhead</note>; for then the strike of the rays creates more acute angles, so that the lines of the rays are closer together; whereas, by contrast, when the sun is at a great slant, the angles are very obtuse, and therefore the lines of the rays are further apart. But in the meantime, it must be noted that there can be many operations of the sun's rays, and even of the nature of heat itself, which are not proportional to our sense of touch; so that, in respect to us, they do not work enough to cause heating—

### To the fifth instance, the tenth observation.

Outpourings and eruptions of flame are found no less in cold regions than in hot ones; as in *Iceland* and *Greenland*. For nothing is found in our experience, whether it be <term>Tangible</term> <note>Solid or liquid matter that can be felt.</note> or <term>Spiritual</term> <note>In 17th-century science, "spiritual" referred to invisible, active substances like air, vapors, or gases, rather than the supernatural.</note>, which does not take on heat when placed near a fire. They differ, however, in that some take on heat more quickly, such as Air, Oil, and Water; while others do so more slowly, such as Stone and Metals. But this subject belongs to the *Table of Degrees* <note>Bacon’s "Table of Degrees" or "Table of Comparison" was his method for ranking how much of a particular quality, like heat, different substances possessed.</note>.

->**To the fifteenth, the twenty-first.**<-
No other Negative Instance is joined to this, except to note carefully that sparks are not produced from flint and steel, or any other hard substance, unless tiny particles are knocked off from the substance of the Stone or Metal itself. Friction of the air never generates sparks on its own, as is commonly believed. Furthermore, those sparks themselves, because of the weight of the ignited matter, tend to fall downward rather than fly upward, and when they go out, they turn back into a kind of physical soot.

->NOVUM ORGANUM. 173<-

<margin>Negative</margin> For no tangible body is found among us that does not manifestly grow hot through friction; so much so that the **Ancients** <note>original: "Veteres" — referring to Greek and Scholastic philosophers like Aristotle</note> dreamed that the Heavenly Bodies possessed no other power or virtue for producing heat except from the friction of the Air through their rapid and hurried rotation. But in this category, further inquiry must be made into whether bodies emitted from **Machines** (such as balls from **Cannons** <note>original: "Tormentis"</note>) do not acquire some degree of heat from the impact itself, so that after they have fallen, they are found to be somewhat warm. Yet, Air in motion cools more than it heats; as seen in winds, bellows, and the breath of a puckered mouth. However, this kind of motion is not so rapid as to excite heat; and it occurs as a whole mass, not by its particles: so it is no wonder if it does not generate heat.

*Regarding the seventeenth, the twenty-third.* <note>These numbers refer to specific instances in Bacon's "Tables of Discovery."</note>

Concerning this Instance, a more diligent inquiry must be made. For green and moist **Herbs** and **Vegetables** seem to possess something of a hidden heat within them. That heat, however, is so subtle that in individual plants it is not perceived by touch: But after they have been gathered together and shut up, so that their <term>spirits</term> <note>In early modern science, "spirits" were considered the invisible, active, and volatile components of matter that directed its growth and decay.</note> do not escape into the air but cherish one another, then indeed a manifest heat arises, and sometimes even a flame in suitable material <note>Bacon is observing the phenomenon of spontaneous combustion or "heating" in haystacks and compost heaps.</note>.

174          VERULAM <note>Referring to Francis Bacon, Baron Verulam.</note>

*Regarding the eighteenth instance, the twenty-fourth.*

A more diligent inquiry must also be made regarding this instance. For it appears that **Quicklime** <term>calx viva: limestone that has been "burned" in a kiln to produce calcium oxide, which is highly reactive</term> conceives heat when sprinkled with water. This seems to happen either because of the concentration of heat that was previously scattered (as was said before regarding enclosed herbs), or because of the irritation and exasperation of the fiery spirit by the water, resulting in a kind of conflict and *antiperistasis* <term>antiperistasis: an ancient and early-modern scientific theory where a quality is intensified when surrounded by its opposite, such as internal heat increasing when surrounded by external cold</term>. Which of these two is the actual cause will be more easily seen if **Oil** is poured on instead of Water. For Oil will serve just as well as Water to concentrate the enclosed spirit, but it will not irritate it. This experiment should also be extended further, both with the ashes and limes of various bodies, and by the addition of various liquids.

*Regarding the nineteenth instance, the twenty-fifth.*

To this instance is added the **Negative** <note>Bacon uses "Negative Instances" to show where a certain nature—in this case, heat—is absent, helping to narrow down the true cause.</note> regarding other metals which are more soft and fluid. For gold leaf dissolved in *aqua regia* <term>aqua regia: literally "royal water," a mixture of nitric and hydrochloric acids used to dissolve noble metals</term> gives off no heat to the touch during its dissolution; nor similarly does Lead in *aqua fortis* <term>aqua fortis: literally "strong water," or nitric acid</term>. Nor does quicksilver (as I recall). However, silver itself excites a little heat, and copper too (as I recall), but more clearly tin, and most of all iron and steel; which not only excite a strong heat during dissolution, but even a vio- <note>The text cuts off mid-word, continuing as "violent" on the following page.</note>

<summary>Bacon explores why quicklime generates heat when wet and compares the heat produced by different metals when dissolved in acids.</summary>

*To the twentieth, the twenty-sixth.* <note>These references link Bacon's "Instances" of heat to their corresponding negative examples (where heat is expected but not found).</note>

To the **Heat of Animals** no Negative instance is joined, except for that of **Insects** (as has been said) on account of the smallness of their bodies. Indeed, in **Fish**, when compared to land animals, a degree of heat <note>original: "coloris" (color), which is almost certainly a printer's error for "caloris" (heat)</note> is noted rather than a total absence. In **Vegetables** and **Plants**, however, no degree of heat is perceived by touch, neither in their "tears" <note>The sap, resins, or gums that bleed from a plant</note> nor in their freshly opened piths. But in **Animals** a great diversity of Heat is found, both in their parts (for the heat is different around the Heart, another in the Brain, and another in the External parts) and in their "accidents" <note>In this context, "accidents" means temporary conditions or circumstances</note>, such as in violent exercise and fevers.

*To the twenty-first, the twenty-seventh.*

To this Instance a Negative is hardly joined. Furthermore, the **excrement of animals**, even when not fresh, clearly possesses potential heat, as is seen in the enriching of the soil <note>original: "impinguatione Solis," likely a typo for "soli" (the soil), referring to how manure "fattens" or fertilizes the ground</note>.

<meta>This page continues Francis Bacon's investigation into the "Form of Heat" from his work *Novum Organum*. Specifically, it continues a list of observations where substances exhibit the properties of heat (like burning or dissolving) without having a high temperature themselves.</meta>

->176 OF VERULAM<-

...which have a great and intense sharpness, perform the actions of heat in the tearing apart of bodies, and even in burning them after a certain delay; yet, to the touch of the hand, they are not hot at the beginning. However, they operate according to the relationship and the pores <note>Bacon uses the word "poros" to describe the microscopic structure of matter, suggesting that chemicals work by fitting into specific gaps in a material's structure.</note> of the body to which they are applied. For <term>King's Water</term> <note>original: "Aqua Regis"; a powerful mixture of nitric and hydrochloric acids so named because it can dissolve "noble" metals.</note> dissolves gold, but silver not at all. On the contrary, <term>Strong Water</term> <note>original: "Aqua fortis"; nitric acid.</note> dissolves silver, but gold not at all. Neither of them dissolves glass. And so it is for other substances.

*Regarding the twenty-fourth instance, the twenty-ninth.*

Let an experiment be made with <term>spirit of wine</term> <note>original: "spiritus vini"; concentrated alcohol or ethanol.</note> on wood, and also on butter, or wax, or pitch, to see if perhaps by its own heat it might liquefy them to some degree. For the twenty-fourth instance showed its power to imitate heat in the way it creates crusts <note>Likely referring to how alcohol can "cook" or harden certain organic tissues.</note>. Therefore, let a similar experiment be performed regarding liquefaction. Also, let an experiment be made using a <term>graduated glass</term> <note>original: "Vitrum Graduum"; an early thermoscope or primitive thermometer used to measure changes in temperature via the expansion of air.</note> or calendar-glass, which has a hollow at its top on the exterior; let well-rectified <note>Purified through distillation.</note> spirit of wine be placed into that exterior hollow, with a lid so that it may better contain its heat; and let it be noted whether by its own heat it causes the water to descend.
